note:
Unlike Matthew and Luke, Mark does not contain an account of Jesus’ birth. The “beginning” (see Gen. 1:1; John 1:1) is identified with the ministry of John the Baptist (see Acts 1:22) and with the OT prophecies announcing John’s coming.

**gospel.** A term from political or personal reporting and correspondence, meaning “good news.” The Greeks used this word for events such as the birth of an emperor or a major military victory.

**of Jesus Christ.** This phrase can be understood as either “about Jesus Christ” or “from Jesus Christ.” The gospel is “about” Jesus, but it is also “from” Him (Rom. 1:9; 1 Cor. 9:12; 2 Cor. 10:14). The gospel of Mark claims divine authority and offers itself as the revelation of Christ through His apostles to the church (see Rev. 1:1).

**Son of God.** Mark presents Jesus at the beginning of the gospel as the divine, eternal Son. See notes on 13:32; 14:36; 15:39; cf. Rom. 1:3.

By placing this citation of the OT here, Mark shows the organic progress of revelation under the divine Lord of history. If the OT is the gospel’s beginning and source, the gospel revealed through Jesus Christ is the final and inspired interpretation and completion of the OT message.

**the prophet.** See text note. The citation is a chain of texts (Ex. 23:20; Is. 40:3; Mal. 3:1) concerning messengers that God sent before John the Baptist and Christ by way of preparation, with Isaiah mentioned specifically because most of the citation is drawn from his prediction. Words drawn from the other OT passages turn the citation into a promise by God the Father to His Son to send “my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way”; this Son is then identified as “the Lord” whose way is being prepared. The references from Exodus and Malachi serve to interpret the text from Isaiah, especially since allusions and quotations from Isaiah dominate the gospel of Mark. Thus, even though Mal. 3:1 is cited first before Isaiah, it functions to explain Isaiah. Mark is concerned throughout his gospel with the second exodus prophesied by Is. 40–54.

The OT citations locate John the Baptist in the preplanned history of God’s covenantal dealings with His people.

**in the wilderness.** John’s preaching in the wilderness symbolically reminds Israel of her covenantal origins in the exodus (see Jer. 2:2). The wilderness is the traditional meeting place between God and His people.

**baptism of repentance.** The Qumran community, which was responsible for copying and preserving the Dead Sea Scrolls, practiced ritual cleansings and baptisms. Also, converts to Judaism were baptized. John’s innovation was to require a one-time baptism of repentance for Israelites already within the covenant community. For him to require such a gesture of radical repentance is a sign of the approach of the new covenant. See note on Matt. 3:6.

**for the forgiveness of sins.** John does not actually bestow forgiveness of sins. Definitive forgiveness of sins belongs to the new covenant (Jer. 31:34) that the Messiah will bring. In the fourth gospel, John the Baptist testifies to Jesus as “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29).
This is literary exaggeration, indicating that the covenant people are going out to John in a great crowd, no doubt as entire families (4:1; 6:44 and notes).
John’s clothing and food identify him as a classic type of OT prophet (2 Kin. 1:8; Zech. 13:4) and connect him particularly to Elijah (Mark 6:14, 15; 9:11–13).

The identity of the One whom John announces and before whom he is unworthy to kneel is evident from the OT prophecies already cited. It is the “Lord” who “will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant,” having been preceded by God’s “messenger” (Mal. 3:1).

The new covenant brings renewal to the people of God (Jer. 31:33, 34; Ezek. 37:14) through the Son and the Holy Spirit, whom the Son possesses in full measure (Is. 42:1; 61:1). The Son fulfills this role by pouring out the Spirit on the day of Pentecost (Acts 1:4, 5; 2:33).

According to John 2:20, one of Jesus’ earliest acts following His baptism took place when the rebuilding of the temple was in its forty-sixth year. Since Herod began reconstruction in 19 B.C., Jesus was baptized in about A.D. 27.

**baptized by John.** Jesus knows this to be part of the divine plan “to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15), by which, in His humanity, He identifies fully with the human condition and begins the process of fulfilling all of God’s commandments so that He can bear the sins of humanity as our sinless and righteous representative. See theological note “The Baptism of Christ” on previous page.

This important word (sometimes translated “straightway”) is characteristic of Mark. It appears twelve times in the rest of the NT, but forty-two times in Mark. Its primary emphasis is not on speed but rather the sureness and inevitability of God’s sovereign plan, recalling the “straight” (same root as “straightway”) paths divinely prepared for Jesus’ coming and ministry (1:3).

**Spirit descending.** This descent of the Spirit is a sign of Jesus’ anointing as the Messiah, His recognition as the promised Davidic king (v. 8 note). Peter refers to this event when he says that “God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:38). In Jesus’ baptism, as later in Christian baptism (Matt. 28:19), all three persons of the Trinity are involved. The initiative of the Father, the vicarious work of the Son, and the glorifying, enabling power of the Spirit are all revealed in this act.

The mystery of the person of Jesus finds expression in the divine declaration. He, the second person of the Godhead, is at the same time the one true and faithful Israel (Ex. 4:23), the Israel who pleases the Father and whom the Father personally and officially acknowledges as Son (Ps. 2:7; Is. 42:1). See note on v. 1.

The verb “drove” is strong, giving the idea of divine and scriptural necessity. The Spirit is driving Jesus out into the “wilderness,” just as Israel, called God’s “son” (Ex. 4:23) and “baptized into Moses ... in the sea” (1 Cor. 10:2; cf. Ex. 14:13–31), was led by the Spirit in the pillars of cloud and fire (Ex. 14:19, 20) along the path of wilderness testing.

Possibly a symbolic reference to the forty years of Israel’s wilderness experience (Deut. 1:3; see v. 12 note) or Moses’s forty-day fast on Mount Sinai (Ex. 34:28).

**wild animals.** This detail emphasizes that the wilderness is a place of curse where the devil is master (Matt. 12:43; see Eph. 2:2). Jesus enters this domain and binds the strong man (see note 3:23–27). This scene recalls the testing of Adam. Although Adam was in a garden and not threatened by wild beasts, he fell to Satan’s tempting. In the wilderness, Jesus, the second Adam, begins His defeat of the devil and His work of redemption by passing the test of filial obedience in a hostile and corrupted environment.

**angels were ministering.** Angels accompanied Israel in the exodus (Ex. 14:19; 23:20; 32:34; 33:2). Jesus’ experience in the wilderness is a type of the Christian’s experience in this world (Heb. 3; 4), which is experienced as Satan’s domain (Eph. 6:12). See note on 10:30.

It is often claimed that the chronology of the first three (Synoptic) Gospels is irreconcilable with that of John for three main reasons: (1) the cleansing of the temple is placed in different periods of Jesus’ ministry (but see 11:15 note); (2) the Synoptic Gospels mention only one visit by Jesus to Jerusalem for the last week of His ministry; and (3) in John, Jesus has an early Judean ministry concurrent with that of John the Baptist (John 3:22–24), while in the Synoptic Gospels Jesus begins His ministry in Galilee. However, in saying that a Galilean ministry begins only after John the Baptist’s arrest, Mark is not denying that there was an earlier Judean ministry; it is simply not part of his story. In other words, Mark is being selective in his account and choosing to pass over certain events in His story that John includes in the fourth gospel. It is not a contradiction; it is choosing not to record certain episodes from Jesus’ life in order to focus on what Mark’s original readers most need to know.

The past times, especially of God’s acts of salvation for His people Israel, reach their climax in this present time of salvation through Jesus.

**the kingdom of God is at hand.** The kingdom of God is that final state of affairs in which God’s supreme reign is fully realized over the transformed universe and in the hearts of all His redeemed and glorified people. This kingdom is “at hand” in the sense that the coming of Jesus sets in motion all that will bring about its actualization. God requires repentance and belief in response to this news. See note on v. 4.
An inland lake thirteen miles (21 km) long and eight miles (13 km) wide, otherwise known in the NT as the Lake of Gennesaret (Luke 5:1) or the Sea of Tiberias (John 6:1).

Mark immediately shows Jesus choosing disciples to follow Him and to call others to Him. This first appointed ministry of the nascent church has as its primary goal seeking the lost. This emphasis on evangelism was not lost on the apostle Paul, who said, “Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel” (1 Cor. 9:16).
Jesus does not recruit His apostles and “fishers of men” from the religious intelligentsia but from ordinary walks of life.
This detail suggests a small, prosperous business.

Jesus’ teaching is unlike that of the scribes because it is tied to His person (2:10) and to His interpretation of Scripture (12:35–40). Note the contrast in the Sermon on the Mount: “You have heard that it was said ... but I say” (e.g., Matt. 5:21, 22). Its content is new, announcing the coming of the kingdom (v. 15) and the defeat of Satan (v. 27).

verse_quote: What have you to do with us.
note:
This idiom distances the speaker from the person addressed. It occurs elsewhere in the NT (Mark 5:7; John 2:4) and in the OT (2 Sam. 16:10; 19:22).

**Nazareth.** Lit. “Nazarene.” Nazareth, west of the Sea of Galilee, is Jesus’ hometown.

**to destroy us.** Jesus’ mission is to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8), and His exorcisms of demons from victims whom they have possessed and tormented is the beginning of God’s royal conquest to vanquish the forces of evil and death.

**Holy One of God.** Jesus is described this way only in this incident (cf. Luke 4:34). The demons quake in the presence of divine holiness.
This strong term emphasizes Jesus’ power to establish His kingdom in the face of evil. With the same term, which can also be rendered “be muzzled,” He will silence the stormy sea (4:39).

See v. 16.

**James and John.** See v. 19.
Peter is married (cf. 1 Cor. 9:5), showing that marriage is normal for Christian leaders. At the same time, celibacy remains a legitimate possibility (Matt. 19:12; 1 Cor. 7:7, 8, 32).
Jesus has already healed on the Sabbath day (v. 25). On this occasion the people wait till sunset, when the Sabbath ends, to carry their sick to Jesus.

The extent of demon possession in Galilee’s Jewish population (v. 32 note) is startling, though the large size of the Gentile or pagan population in Galilee must not be forgotten.

**he would not permit the demons to speak.** This is the first instance in Mark of what has been called the “messianic secret” (v. 43; 3:12; 4:10, 11; 5:19, where Jesus permits Gentiles to hear of Him because they will not jeopardize His mission by their acclaim; 8:30; 9:9). The revelation of Jesus as the Jewish Messiah must begin discreetly and proceed by stages so that God’s plan for the death of His Servant will not be jeopardized by any excesses of popular enthusiasm. Jesus’ aversion to publicity fulfills the profile of the Lord’s servant in Is. 42 (cf. Matt. 12:18–21).
Lit. “deserted place,” where Jesus fights His spiritual battle (v. 12; see v. 3). As with ancient Israel, it is also a type of the present Christian walk (1 Cor. 10:1–11; Heb. 13:12, 13).

verse_quote: for that is why I came out.
note: He has come out not only from Capernaum but also from His Father in heaven. Jesus states His program of evangelistic preaching with compelling clarity. He says in Luke 19:10, “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” He is on the move, touring Galilee several times (v. 39; 6:6; Luke 8:1).

Under the Mosaic law, certain skin diseases make a person ceremonially unclean, excluding him from communal life (Lev. 13:46). Living under the Mosaic covenant, this leper is unclean and an outcast from society.
Jesus’ pity and compassion will move Him not only to cleanse this outcast but also to feed the hungry (6:30–44; 8:1–10) and release a boy from demonic torment (9:22).
See note on v. 34. The Gk. verb expresses deep emotion, even anger, as in the case of Jesus before the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:33, 38).

Jesus respects the Mosaic law as the great high priest of a line other than Aaron’s (Heb. 7:11–8:13), but He is not bound or limited by it. Although touching the leper is a violation of the laws of ritual purity (Lev. 5:3), Jesus does so as He heals him. Whereas under the law defilement is contagious, in the case of Jesus, His purity imparts cleanness to the defiled.

This is not the time for unbridled proclamation (v. 34 note), though there will come a time in the history of redemption (after the resurrection) when open preaching will be proper (Matt. 10:27; Luke 12:2, 3).

**desolate places.** Again, Jesus exerts the power of God’s kingdom in uninhabited wilderness areas. See notes on vv. 3, 4, 12, 35.

Jesus is from Nazareth, about twenty miles (32 km) away, and Simon Peter’s house (1:29) may be serving as His home in Capernaum, a village more centrally located and with direct access to the Sea of Galilee.
First-century houses in Galilee had flat roofs made of branches and dried clay supported by wooden beams.

Jesus’ response is extraordinary for two reasons. First, the man has come for healing of a physical disability, but Jesus speaks about the more profound defect of sin and about the radical healing of forgiveness, of which this particular physical healing is a sign. Second, Jesus claims for Himself the power to forgive sins, which in all the Bible can be attributed only to God (Ex. 34:7; Is. 1:18; see Ps. 51:4). The teachers of the law immediately accuse Jesus of “blaspheming” (v. 7; 3:29 note), a proper conclusion only if He is a mere man.

Jesus asks the scribes to reconsider their judgment in the light of His power to heal (cf. John 5:36; 10:25, 38), which is ultimately a divine power (Ps. 41:1; Jer. 3:22; Hos. 14:4). The dilemma He poses shows that both forgiveness and instantaneous healing such as He is about to perform are far beyond human capacities but well within the power of God, “who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases” (Ps. 103:3).

Jesus uses this phrase regularly to designate Himself, associating Himself in His ministry with the heavenly “Son of Man” of Dan. 7:13, 14 (v. 28; 8:31; 9:31; 10:33, 45; 13:26). See note on Matt. 8:20.

**authority on earth.** Daniel’s vision showed the heavenly exaltation of the Son of Man and will be fulfilled in Jesus’ ascension (14:62; Acts 1:9), but Jesus is already exerting the divine and kingly authority of the Son of Man’s prophesied reign in His earthly humiliation by forgiving sins on the ground of the sacrifice He will offer on the cross.

This person is named “Matthew” in the parallel account in Matt. 9:9–13. Since Matthew appears in Mark’s list of apostles (3:18) and there is no mention of Levi, it appears that Levi was also called “Matthew,” and it was by that name that he was best known in the early church.

**tax booth.** Tax booths were set up on highways, bridges, and canals for tolls and at the lakeside to tax fishing. See note on Luke 3:12. Tax collectors were despised by their fellow first-century Jews for their collaboration with Rome’s occupying forces and extorting higher-than-justified levies to enrich themselves dishonestly. By seeking out and enlisting Levi, Jesus demonstrates the shocking mercy of God toward the most undeserving people, even those on the margins of society (Luke 18:9–14; 19:1–10).

**he rose.** The radical demand of Jesus’ call and the unconditional obedience of the one who hears are thrown into sharp relief for the reader.

A term of disdain used by the Pharisees for all Jews who do not follow their traditions of legal purity, both moral and ritual.

**reclining with.** Contact with sinners is seen as defiling Jesus, since rabbinic regulations specifically prohibit such table fellowship. On the other hand, the “sinners” will see in this a gesture of friendship and acceptance (14:20 note).

Theological descendants of the Hasidim, a second-century B.C. movement of piety, learning, and faithfulness to the Mosaic law against Greek pagan influence. At the time of Jesus, strict observance of the law, and especially ritual purity, was regulated by a body of ethical teachings known as “the tradition of the elders” (7:3), developed by the Pharisees as an application of the law to specific situations. The difficulty of knowing this tradition and all its many subtle interpretations created a social and religious gap between a sanctimonious elite, “the righteous,” and the general population, “the sinners.”

Note the clear declaration of the priority of His mission (see 1:38). There is both truth and biting irony in Jesus’ words. Tax collectors, prostitutes, and the like are indeed spiritually “sick,” but Jesus does not really intend the Pharisees to think of themselves as “healthy” (see Luke 18:9–14). Jesus is breaking down the artificial categories of legalistic, works-righteousness religion. Like the OT (Ps. 14:1–3), Jesus teaches that all are sinners (Mark 7:1–8) and that righteousness is first and foremost a gift of God to repentant sinners (Ps. 51:1–18; Luke 19:9; Rom. 3:22).

The Mosaic law requires only one fast annually, on the Day of Atonement (Lev. 16:29–31; see Acts 27:9, which calls this day “the Fast”). Nevertheless, as a sign of contrition and penitence associated with prayer, fasting was a part of OT piety from the time of the judges (Judg. 20:26; 1 Kin. 21:27), sometimes becoming an empty ritual (Is. 58:3). The Pharisees and their adherents apparently fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12). Since the message of John the Baptist centered on repentance (Matt. 3:11), fasting was appropriate for his disciples. Jesus, whose own message included repentance, does not insist upon fasting as a constant practice, but does instruct His disciples about the proper spirit in which to fast (Matt. 6:16–18).

The reason that Jesus gives sets Him off from all that has come before Him, for the “bridegroom” has now come, the “new” (vv. 21, 22) is present. By comparing Himself to the bridegroom, Jesus affirms the presence of the kingdom as a time for celebration, like a wedding. Jesus eats and drinks with publicans and sinners, bringing joy and salvation to them (Luke 19:6, 9). John the Baptist likewise compares Jesus to the long-awaited bridegroom whose arrival brings joy (John 3:29).
The present celebration (v. 19) is provisional, for Jesus has yet to suffer and die, and “the bridegroom [will be] taken away from them.” See Acts 13:2; 14:23.

The images of new cloth and new wineskins again emphasize the new situation brought about by the coming of the kingdom and of its king. As symbols of unwise actions, they show the inappropriateness of fasting, a form of the old order, in this new situation., 22

The problem with the legalistic reasoning by certain Pharisees is illustrated in this incident. The disciples were not stealing or doing farm work but were benefiting from a provision of the law of Moses whereby those in need were permitted to glean small amounts of grain from fields to satisfy their hunger (Lev. 23:22; Deut. 23:25). Their accusers counted even plucking the “heads of grain” as reaping, which was prohibited on the Sabbath (Ex. 34:21).

Jesus’ question suggests an ironic criticism of their knowledge of Scripture (John 3:10; 5:39, 47). Jesus does not justify Himself by laying Scripture aside. He rather shows His understanding of its depth and its proper application to human need.

**David.** Executing a divine mission (1 Sam. 21:5) as the Lord’s anointed, David ate the consecrated bread normally reserved for the priests (Lev. 24:9). Jesus, as the Son of David and final Anointed One, allows His disciples to fulfill their physical needs so they might continue their mission of redemption, a work of necessity that is always lawful.

According to 1 Sam. 21:1–6, it was Abiathar’s father, Ahimelech, who gave David the consecrated bread. However, Abiathar was certainly alive, and perhaps even present, when the incident referred to occurred. So the phrase “in the time of Abiathar” is strictly correct. Probably Jesus refers to Abiathar because he is so well known among the Jews of His day as one of David’s chief supporters.

(see v. 10). Jesus declares His authority as the Son of Man who brings blessings, this time as the Mediator of the OT law concerning the Sabbath. This claim is made against traditions that have turned the life-promoting fourth commandment (Ex. 20:8–11) into a burden. Since the Sabbath was instituted at creation and not only under Moses, the Lord of the Sabbath is also Lord of creation.

This is not a life-and-death illness, the healing of which is permitted on the Sabbath by the rules of the Pharisees (v. 4 note). Jesus’ action appears to be a deliberate provocation as well as an act of mercy.
The Pharisees (v. 6) make Jesus’ action a test case, as Jesus evidently wants them to do.

Jesus anticipates their criticism by reiterating the Sabbath teaching He began in 2:25–28. Jesus shows that the Pharisees’ interpretation of the Sabbath law is against the spirit of the commandment, which is the promotion of goodness and wholeness (2:27). The good that Jesus does in bringing redemption is required, not forbidden, by the divine law.

A nonreligious, political group supporting the dynasty of the Herods. They supported and depended upon this dynasty’s alliance with Rome. In collaborating with the Herodians, the Pharisees have moved far from the OT ideal for the people of God (see Deut. 17:15). For more on this conspiracy, see 8:15; 12:13.

**how to destroy him.** This early in his narrative, well before Jesus’ explicit predictions of His suffering (8:31), Mark shows readers that the cross casts its dark shadow over Christ’s earthly ministry.

The phrase is repeated twice (vv. 7, 8). Jesus’ public ministry, in spite of the opposition of the ruling elite (v. 6), is becoming a mass movement. Jesus is so crowded that He must take refuge in a small boat (v. 9). People are coming to Galilee from everywhere to hear Him.

verse_quote: whenever the unclean spirits saw him.
note: Although the crowds are Jewish (see 7:26–29), Jesus is constantly meeting people possessed with evil spirits. In the presence of Jesus, the true nature of the combat (Eph. 6:12) becomes evident. The demons are exposed, and they expose the true identity of Jesus, the Son of God (1:1; 15:39 and notes).
Mark emphasizes that the choice of the apostles has its origin in Jesus’ determined purpose.

In such a context, the significance of the number twelve can hardly be missed. Jesus is setting up the constitution of the renewed Israel (Matt. 19:28).

**apostles.** From a Gk. verb meaning “to send,” this title designates official representatives and spokesmen who wield delegated authority on behalf of the Lord who sends them (Luke 10:16). See theological note “The Apostles” on p. 1912.

**that they might be with him.** A signal point of the uniqueness of the Twelve is the time they spend with the earthly Jesus, a time of preparation (Acts 1:21–22; 4:13).

**preach.** Again (1:14, 17) the priority is a preaching mission coupled with exorcism. The time of preparation has a markedly practical emphasis.

Mark 3:16–19 and Matt. 10:2–4 list identical names for the Twelve. The parallel list in Luke 6:12–16 (see Acts 1:13) has “Judas” instead of “Thaddaeus.” A possible explanation of this difference is that Thaddaeus had a second name, Judas.

**Zealot.** See note on Matt. 10:4.

Some believe that Judas was a political revolutionary because “Iscariot” may be derived from the Latin _itsicarius_, meaning“assassin.” More likely, the word has a Semitic origin: _ish_ meaning “man (of),” and _Kerioth_, a town in Israel close to Hebron (Josh. 15:25).

**who betrayed him.** Another foreshadowing of Jesus’ coming suffering, in which one of His inner circle will be complicit (14:10, 11, 43–45).

Some interpreters identify these as Jesus’ family; others propose associates or friends (the Gk. expression is “those connected to Him”). However, the group is probably identified in v. 31 as “his mother and his brothers.”

**out of his mind.** The phrase expresses unbelief toward Jesus by those who are closest to Him, humanly speaking (John 7:5), although Mary’s perspective may be more complex (Luke 2:19, 51; John 2:3–5).
Gk. _beelzeboul,_ the god of Ekron (2 Kin. 1:2; Matt. 10:25 note). The Pharisees use it as a name for Satan and accuse Jesus of casting out demons by the power of Satan.

See note on 4:2. This parable illustrates Jesus’ claim that the kingdom of God has come (Matt. 12:28), for one stronger than the “strong man” is here, able to bind Satan and to free people from his kingdom. The Gk. term translated “bind” reappears in Rev. 20:2–4, a vision in which Satan is bound, preventing him from continuing to deceive the nations.

For various forms of blasphemy, see 2:7; Ex. 22:28; Lev. 24:10–16; Ezek. 35:12, 13; John 10:33–36; Acts 6:11. The unforgivable blasphemy specified here is the act of deliberately attributing the power and the work of Jesus, who is full of the Holy Spirit, to the work of Satan. This is to equate supreme spiritual good with supreme spiritual evil, evidencing a hardened heart that is incapable of being forgiven because it is incapable of repentance and faith. See theological note “The Unforgivable Sin” on previous page.

See v. 21 and note. Roman Catholic commentators, for whom the perpetual virginity of Mary is a dogma, stress that “brother” can refer to wider family relations, pointing to Gen. 13:8; 14:16; Lev. 10:4; 1 Chr. 23:22. However, in Mark the term always seems to mean siblings from the same parents. Matt. 1:25 implies that Mary and Joseph began normal marital relations after the birth of Jesus, giving added meaning to Luke’s designation of Jesus as Mary’s “firstborn” (Luke 2:7). Note the naming of Jesus’ brothers and the mention of His sisters in 6:3.

verse_quote: For whoever does the will of God.
note: The arrival of the kingdom of God changes human relationships. Those who oppose its progress, whether mothers or brothers, must be left behind; those in the kingdom become a person’s closest associates, nearer and dearer than any others.
See note on Matt. 13:3.

In first-century Palestine, sowing preceded plowing. Paths made by villagers would not be plowed, and the seed that fell there was wasted. Rocky places, covered by a thin layer of soil, became visible only after plowing.

See also v. 23; Matt. 11:15; 13:9, 43; Luke 8:8; 14:35; Rev. 2:7; cf. Ps. 115:6. This phrase is a call for close attention. Parables release their meaning only to those who invest in humble meditation and only by God’s sovereign gift of insight into the secret of His kingdom (4:11).
Jesus is alone with His disciples, in particular with the Twelve (3:14 note) giving them special instruction. This aspect of Jesus’ earthly ministry is in all the Gospels.

The “secret” refers to special divine revelation (Rom. 16:25; Eph. 1:9; 3:3, 9), and has reference to the OT notion of the prophet, who by the Spirit is present in God’s deliberative council. What the prophet hears becomes his authoritative, divinely inspired message for the people (Ex. 24:15–18; Deut. 33:2; 1 Kin. 22:19; Is. 6:1–13; Jer. 23:18; Amos 3:7). Such revelation reaches its fulfillment in the gospel, which Paul calls “the mystery of Christ” (Eph. 3:4; Col. 4:3) or “the mystery of the gospel” (Eph. 6:19). Here, the mystery is that the kingdom comes with Jesus because He is the King, even as it arrives in a subtle, vulnerable form—like seed subject to snatching, withering heat, and choking thorns. This “mystery,” revealed to the disciples, is contrasted with “parables” told to “those who are outside.” To those outside, the parable is a riddle (cf. John 16:29), veiling their understanding as the Scripture has prophesied (v. 12, citing Is. 6:9, 10). To them Jesus remains a provocative enigma, as He will throughout His ministry.

This explanation applies to all of Jesus’ parables. See note on Matt. 13:13. The parable of the sower, like the agricultural parables in vv. 26–32 (cf. Matt. 13:24–30, 36–42), teaches that although John’s message (Luke 3:7–9, 16, 17) may have led to expectations that the King’s arrival will immediately effect a harvest of last judgment (Joel 3:9–16), in His first coming He inaugurates the kingdom in patient, redemptive mercy, reserving ultimate justice for His return.

The “mystery” of the parable is not its moral teaching about the hardness of human hearts (on the nature and OT background of “mystery” and its use here in relation to the parables about the kingdom, see Matt. 13:11, 12 note). The “mystery” is to be found in the paradox that the coming of God’s reign is identified with a fragile seed. The Son of Man who exercises all authority on earth (2:11, 27, 28) appears as Jesus of Nazareth. The coming of the kingdom is not equally visible to everyone, although it is a kingdom of power. Those on the outside have unreceptive hearts, exhibited in various ways. For those with ears to hear, the parable unveils the “mystery” of redemption, hidden in the person and work of Christ Himself (1:34 note).

During Christ’s earthly ministry, things are hidden. But the day will come, from the resurrection on, when all will begin to be revealed (Matt. 10:26, 27; Luke 12:2, 3). In particular, the ultimate purpose of His parables is not to conceal God’s light but to display it.

This general principle, which Jesus invokes elsewhere to encourage generosity (Luke 6:38) and humble leniency (Matt. 7:2), here applies to extracting the meaning of parables, which requires a serious investment of prayerful reflection.
This principle is illustrated in the parables of the talents (Matt. 25:14–30) and of the minas (Luke 19:11–27).
The parable of the mustard seed illustrates that the kingdom’s present manifestation in the person of Jesus, which appears negligible, will issue in widespread, global fruition in the future.
In Dan. 4:21, the same metaphor refers to the worldwide dominion of Nebuchadnezzar.
According to 3:7, Jesus is in Galilee. The “other side” of the lake is the region of the Gadarenes in the Decapolis, on the lake’s eastern shore (5:1 note).

The Sea of Galilee is about seven hundred feet (213 m) below sea level, thirteen miles (21 km) long, and eight miles (8 km) wide. At its southern end is a deep, cliff-lined valley. The wind funneling through the surrounding hills and through this valley can whip the lake into sudden violent storms. The crisis resembles the scenes of desperate sailors caught in a storm of wind and waves at sea portrayed in Ps. 107:23–32 and Jon. 1:4–16.

Jesus has been teaching all day and is no doubt exhausted. Mark, like John (John 4:6; 11:35, 38), emphasizes the full humanity of Jesus. On the OT background of Jesus’ “sleep,” see note on Matt. 8:24.

**do you not care.** Their shock when Jesus stills the wind and waves shows their lack of faith in Jesus’ power and in His concern for them. Their panicky question betrays their lack of the kind of confidence expressed earlier by a leper: “If you will, you can make me clean” (1:40).

Lit. “be muzzled.” Jesus has authority on earth to forgive sins (2:10); He is Lord of the Sabbath (2:28); He has authority in His teaching (1:22) and over the demons (1:27); and now He demonstrates His authority over nature. This calming of the storm resembles His exorcisms, with the demonic expression of violence (4:37; cf. 1:26; 5:4, 13), the command to be “silent” (4:39; cf. 1:25 note), and the resultant calm (4:39; cf. 5:15). Jesus binds “the strong man” (3:23–27) and reclaims from his power the physical creation.

Unlike the seamen of Ps. 107:30, but like the pagan sailors who threw Jonah overboard (Jon. 1:16), the disciples feel greater fear in Jesus’ presence on the calm sea than they experienced while the storm raged.

**Who then is this.** Ps. 107:28, 29 answers the disciples’ question: “Then they cried out to the Lord in their trouble... . He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed.”

Gerasa is thirty miles (48 km) southeast of the lake. There is also a village named Khersa on the eastern shore with the kind of cliffs and tombs described in the story. Jesus enters the Decapolis, a political association of ten independent Greek city-states, anticipating the future Gentile mission of the church. The Gentile character of the population is apparent since first-century Jews did not raise pigs, for they are unclean under Mosaic law.
This demon-possessed man has been exiled from normal human contacts, separated from his village and family (v. 19), preferring the company of the dead (Is. 65:2–5).

Violence and unusual physical strength leading to slow self-destruction (v. 5; 9:22) often seem to characterize the demon possessed (v. 13; 1:26; 9:18, 20, 22, 26; see Rev. 9:4–6). But before the spiritual strength of Jesus, the demons cower and flee (see Jesus’ “binding” analogy in 3:27).

verse_quote: What have you to do with me.

note:
In the first century, naming someone was believed to be a way of gaining power over the one named. The demons have already identified Jesus (v. 7; see 1:24, 34), but by this question Jesus reveals His superior power.

**Legion.** Jesus forces the demon to unmask himself. He is not one but many. A Roman legion consisted of six thousand men.
The demon cowers before Jesus, even invoking God’s name as a form of protection (v. 7), recognizing that Jesus has absolute power over him.

Jesus permits the demons to enter the pigs—unclean spirits into unclean animals. The swine then hurl themselves over the cliff into the sea, returning the demons to their prison in the abyss. This exorcism is a dramatic demonstration of Jesus’ power over evil (vv. 14, 16) and of the presence of the kingdom in His ministry (Luke 11:20). See theological note “Demons” on p. 299.

In comparison with his previous violent behavior and the recent destruction of the pigs, the man “sitting there, clothed and in his right mind” gives eloquent expression to the peace and life-giving restoration that comes from Jesus’ power (4:39; 9:26, 27).

verse_quote: began to beg Jesus to depart.
note: Instead of rejoicing in the demoniac’s freedom and sanity, the Gerasenes seek to put distance between themselves and Jesus’ invasive and disturbing power and purity.

This man becomes the first Gentile missionary. Jesus previously demanded silence (1:34 note), but in this instance He allows the preparation for the future mission of the church to begin. Jesus will later command silence regarding a healing performed in the Decapolis, but to no avail (7:31–37).
Back into Galilee, more heavily populated by Jews than by Gentiles (unlike the Decapolis).

Though he was a layman, Jairus’s responsibilities were socially and religiously important, including not only the upkeep of the building but also the proper conduct of the service and the choice of Torah readings.

The woman’s condition was not only physically debilitating; it also disqualified her from marriage (Lev. 20:18) and religious life in general (Lev. 15:25–33). “Discharge of blood” is more literally translated as “flow of blood,” an allusion to Lev. 15:25, where a woman with a “flow of blood” is “impure” and “unclean” and so unqualified for worship in the tabernacle, and later the temple.

**for twelve years.** The defiled woman’s disability has lasted as long as the dying daughter’s entire life (v. 42).

verse_quote: came up behind him in the crowd.
note: Not surprisingly, the woman in Mark 5 touches Jesus’ garment from behind, fearing others’ disapproval (or worse) if she is seen mixing with ceremonially “clean” people and reaching out to “defile” Jesus as He walks to the synagogue ruler’s home.

verse_quote: If I touch even his garments.
note: Possible superstition notwithstanding (Acts 5:15, 16; 19:11, 12), her faith is strong, putting to shame the disciples’ earlier cowardice (Mark 4:40) and the unbelieving laughter of the mourners in Jairus’s house (5:39, 40).
See note on 1:10.
Jesus felt the woman’s touch, the outward evidence of her faith, even though in such a dense crowd many people were touching Him. The phrase “power had gone out from him” occurs only here.
The disciples’ observation underscores the difference between mere proximity to Jesus and the trust that reaches out to Him for rescue.
A social outcast for many years, her healing is complete only when Jesus publicly identifies her, commends her faith, and declares to all that she is healed (v. 34) and cleansed.

Jesus built around Himself a hierarchy of closeness. There are numerous disciples (4:10) from whom twelve are appointed apostles (3:13–19), and within the Twelve some (Peter, James, John, and sometimes Andrew) enjoy Jesus’ fullest intimacy, most notably at the transfiguration (9:2–13) and in Gethsemane (14:32, 33).
In Middle Eastern cultures, wailing is a customary expression of grief, sometimes calling for professional mourners.

Of course the earlier report (v. 35) was correct; the girl had in fact died. But in the presence of Jesus, the Lord of life, death is no more irreversible than sleep (John 11:11–15; 1 Thess. 4:13–18).

Jesus is not interested in a grand spectacle of healing. Rather, He is concerned for the suffering of the girl, the faith of her parents, and the ultimate goal of His mission (v. 43). In these respects, these actions are in keeping with the nature of the kingdom and its progress during Jesus’ earthly ministry (see 4:14–20, 30–32).

Aramaic was the popular language spoken in Palestine in Jesus’ day. Mark gives the translation for other Aramaic terms (3:17; 7:11, 34; 14:36; 15:22, 34) to clarify his narrative for those unfamiliar with that language.

See notes on v. 19 and 1:34.

**something to eat.** Jesus’ attention to the girl’s need for food and the fact that she immediately begins walking (v. 42) demonstrate the complete restoration effected by her resurrection from the dead.

Nazareth, some twenty miles (32 km) southwest of Capernaum and the Sea of Galilee.

**his disciples.** The Twelve (v. 7).

Although He is Lord of the Sabbath (2:28), Jesus observes weekly Sabbath worship (1:21; 3:1; Luke 4:16–30).

**astonished.** See 1:22; 7:37; 10:26; 11:18.

Can also mean “builder.” Jesus’ work in this occupation before His ministry might explain His use of building metaphors, especially when describing His own ministry (14:58; 15:29; cf. Matt. 7:24; 16:18; 21:33; Luke 12:18; 17:28). The remark concerning manual labor is probably not derogatory as such, for all rabbis in that day were expected to have a trade. For example, Paul had been trained as a rabbi and was a maker of tents or awnings (Acts 18:3; 22:3; 26:5; Phil. 3:5, 6). The accusation being made against Jesus in this verse is that He (who teaches “wisdom” in v. 2) is a common worker without religious or academic credentials.

**son of Mary.** See 3:31. Since men are ordinarily identified by their father’s names in this era, the suggestion may be that, though Joseph protected Mary’s reputation by (chastely) marrying her while she was expecting the birth of her firstborn, pejorative rumors have been circulating concerning the circumstances of Jesus’ conception in the virgin’s womb.

**his sisters.** The identification of Jesus as the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon, as well as the mention of his sisters, most naturally implies that these are all biological children born to Mary and Joseph after Mary gave birth to Jesus.
Not only is Jesus rejected by the people of the town and the wider circle of relatives there but also by His own family (3:21).
The Lord’s sovereign power is not rendered impotent by human unbelief, but refusal to trust Him deprives people of the blessings of His presence and His favor.

Having already been appointed to be with Jesus (3:14 note) and having received special instruction concerning the mystery of His person and role (4:10, 11 notes), the Twelve are now permitted to share His ministry and authority.

**send them out.** The verb has the same root as the Gk. noun translated “apostle” and underlines their link with Jesus as His personal representatives (3:14 note).

**two by two.** The biblical principle that testimony should be established by at least two witnesses (Num. 35:30; Deut. 17:6; 19:15; Matt. 18:16; John 8:17; 2 Cor. 13:1; 1 Tim. 5:19; Heb. 10:28) is also reflected in the missionary activity of the early church in the ministries of Peter and John (Acts 3:1; 4:1), Paul and Barnabas (Acts 13:2), and Paul and Silas (Acts 15:40).

Matt. 10:10 gives the reason: “The laborer deserves his food.” The list of articles not to be taken varies slightly in Matthew (which excludes even staff and sandals), but the point remains that Jesus’ emissaries are to travel light, depending wholly on God’s provision for their daily needs. This fact confirms the provision and temporary nature of this particular mission (see Luke 22:35–38).
In the first century, strict Jews shook the foreign dust from their feet after travel in pagan territories. Refusal of the gospel invites the same reaction (Acts 13:51).
Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, was tetrarch (ruler of a dependent state) of Galilee and Perea.

Speculation about the identity of Jesus will lead to the accounts of the miraculous feedings (vv. 30–44; 8:1–9) and walking on water (vv. 47–52), all of which point to Jesus’ personal divinity. But first Mark will relate the circumstances of the death of John the Baptist, with whom Herod and others have identified Jesus. Jesus will ask His disciples to survey the popular theories about His identity to set up the contrast to Peter’s true confession, “You are the Christ,” at the turning point in this gospel (8:27–29).

Herodias was a daughter of Aristobulus, one of the sons of Herod the Great. Other sons of Herod the Great included Herod Antipas and Herod Philip (by different wives). After marrying her half-uncle Herod Philip, Herodias left him for an adulterous relationship with his brother Herod Antipas. Such were the loose morals, typical of the Herodian dynasty, against which John the Baptist preached (see Lev. 18:16, 20).

verse_quote: Herod feared John ... was greatly perplexed ... heard him gladly.
note: The te­trarch’s ambivalent reaction to John, “a righteous and holy man,” is an extreme expression of a more widespread tendency to hear God’s Word while refusing to respond appropriately to it (Acts 24:22–26; James 1:22–27).

By contrast, none of Jesus’ close disciples claim His body after His death. Instead Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the Sanhedrin who is “looking for the kingdom of God” performs this act of devotion (15:43).
Being alone with Jesus, who then instructs them in the mystery of the kingdom (4:10, 11), is part of their preparation for future ministry (4:34; 9:2, 28; 13:3; cf. John 13:1; 16:29).
Again the wilderness is the venue for Jesus’ instruction and exhibition of the kingdom’s coming.

Jesus does what God promised to do in Ezek. 34:11, 14: “I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out... . I will feed them with good pasture.” Jesus acts as the shepherd of God’s people, like Moses (Num. 27:15–17; Ps. 77:20), David (Ps. 78:70–72), and God Himself (Ps. 23:1; 74:1; 78:52, 53; 80:1; Ezek. 34:15). See John 10:1–30; Heb. 13:20; 1 Pet. 5:1, 2; Rev. 7:17.

**sheep without a shepherd.** Ancient Israel, abandoned by unfaithful leaders, was also described in this way (Jer. 50:6; Ezek. 34:1–10).
This detail recalls the ordering of ancient Israel in the wilderness under Moses (Ex. 18:21).
This feeding story recalls the miraculous provision of manna in the wilderness under Moses (Ex. 16:1–36, esp. v. 16). Jesus is the new Moses bringing the new covenant (John 6:30–51).

A further reference to the provision of manna in which nothing was to be left until morning (Ex. 16:19).

**twelve baskets full.** The number recalls the twelve tribes of ancient Israel and may suggest the important role that the Twelve play in the constitution of the new Israel (3:14 note).

Mark does not use the Gk. word that means “human being” but a term distinguishing men from women, with perhaps the idea of “head of family” (cf. “besides women and children” in Matt. 14:21). The total crowd may actually number between fifteen thousand and twenty thousand.
Since the Romans divided the night into four periods, the fourth watch was the three hours ending at dawn.
Lit. “phantasm,” used in the NT only here and in Matt. 14:26. It has the connotation of superstitious imagination.

The Gk. phrase (lit. “I am”) likely alludes to the Septuagint’s rendering of the divine name “I am” revealed to Moses (Ex. 3:14; Deut. 32:39; Is. 41:4; 43:10, 13, 25; 45:18; 52:6; Hos. 13:4; Joel 2:27). On another occasion, the claim to deity implicit in this expression is recognized even by unbelieving Jewish listeners (John 8:58, 59; 10:30–33). This account has all the usual marks of biblical theophany narratives (various modes of visible, divine self-revelation), including human dread, divine identification, and words of assurance. One psalmist recalls Israel’s departure from Egypt, when God’s “way was through the sea, your path through the great waters, yet your footprints were unseen” (Ps. 77:19; cf. Hab. 3:15).

verse_quote: they did not understand about the loaves.
note: This remark suggests that the miracle of the feeding contains the same mystery concerning Jesus as does His walking on water. Jesus, as to His humanity, is indeed the new Moses. But He is at the same time the God who provided bread from heaven (Ex. 16:4).
A village on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee (Luke 5:1).
See note on 5:30.

Jesus’ confrontation with the Pharisees exposes their corruption of the meaning of Scripture by their traditions that they place on the same level as the Word of God. In correcting the Pharisees, Jesus demonstrates the final authority of Scripture over all traditions of men, even traditions born from good intentions.

**7:1 Pharisees.** See note on 2:16.

**scribes.** Scribes were teachers of the law, often Pharisees (see 2:16, “the scribes of the Pharisees”).

The disciples have not washed in the manner prescribed by “the tradition of the elders” (vv. 3, 4) and so are considered ceremonially unclean. Jesus is critical of these traditional expansions of the ceremonial law by the scribes and Pharisees because they have so extended their traditions as to permit actual transgression of the moral law (vv. 9–13). His cross will finally bring the ceremonial law to an end.

By their tradition, the Pharisees have extended the biblical injunctions for priestly washing at the moment of temple sacrifice (Ex. 30:19; 40:12) to the eating of bread by all Jews in their homes.

**tradition of the elders.** The Pharisees believe that in addition to the written words of the law, Moses received instructions for its interpretation and application. This oral law was passed on by word of mouth from teacher to teacher. In His arguments with them, Jesus consistently appeals to Scripture and always leads them back to its true meaning (vv. 6–8).
The Pharisees and scribes are not genuinely interested in the meal practice of the disciples but in why Jesus, as their teacher, does not require them to observe “the tradition” generally.

Jesus’ motivation is to bring people back into conformity with Scripture.

**hypocrites ... their lips ... their heart.** The disjunction between one’s verbal expressions and one’s heart allegiance is the essence of hypocrisy. It may manifest itself in elevating human expectations while devaluing or evading God’s revealed standards.

The Gk. verb translated as “leave” can mean “cancel,” “abandon,” or “neglect.” Jesus is not an antinomian. Like the psalmist, He is consumed with longing for the law of God (Ps. 119:20), which He fulfills, protects (Matt. 5:17–20), and defends. He is not even against all tradition, but only that which annuls Scripture.

A Hebrew and Aramaic word (which Mark translates for his Gentile readers), designating something as dedicated to a religious purpose. By a simple vow to reserve their possessions as a gift to God, people could avoid responsibility to support their parents. The fifth commandment obligates adult children as well as minors, and it enjoins concrete assistance for parents as well as an attitude of respect.

verse_quote: Thus he declared all foods clean.
note:
This parenthetical comment, not in Matthew’s version, may preserve a conclusion expressed orally by Peter, who is later taught this lesson by heavenly vision before being sent to preach to Cornelius (Acts 10, 11). In any case, it is an inference subsequently drawn from Jesus’ reply to the Pharisees.

**The Ministry of Jesus Beyond Galilee**

verse_quote: What comes out of a person.
note:
Jesus is generalizing about the natural and constant way in which fallen human nature is expressed, and His list of vices (vv. 21, 22) is meant to bring horrifying self-knowledge (cf. Rom. 1:24–32; 2:17–24).

**defiles.** Jesus goes to the essence of the matter—uncleanness of the heart, of which ceremonial uncleanness is really a symbol.

verse_quote: out of the heart of man.
note: Jesus expands the discussion beyond food that enters the mouth and words that emerge from it, tracing all sorts of sinful actions to the spiritual corruption within. Only deep and radical cleansing, performed by God Himself (Deut. 30:6; Ps. 51:7, 17; Ezek. 36:25–27), can remove such intrinsic defilement.

Jesus moves north into a markedly Gentile region (see Matt. 11:21, 22), to the vicinity of the ancient Phoenician port city of Tyre (in modern Lebanon) and the region of Elijah’s sojourn with a widow in Zarephath (1 Kin. 17:8–24).
She is of Syrian descent but speaks Greek.

Though in Gentile territory, Jesus maintains the temporal priority of Israel (“the children”) in the divine plan of salvation, as Paul does later (Rom. 1:16; 2:10; cf. Acts 1:8; 13:46, 47).

**dogs.** The term is certainly derogatory (Matt. 7:6; Phil. 3:2; Rev. 22:15), though the Gk. word includes the nuance “little dogs” or “pets.” It should be seen as an example of Jesus’ colorful imagery of table fellowship to explain the plan of salvation, namely, that “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22). The woman takes it in this sense, as her reply indicates that she is not deterred by His implicit reminder of Israel’s special covenant with the living God.

Boldly engaging Jesus’ dinner-table metaphor, the Syro­phoenician woman confesses her confidence that the mercy Jesus has to give will more than fill the needs of those within God’s covenant community and therefore spill out to meet Gentiles’ needs as well—another anticipation of the church’s global mission following Jesus’ death, resurrection, ascension, and outpouring of the Spirit.
See note on 5:1. Jesus remains in Gentile territory, first going north to Sidon and then southeast, around the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee, to the Decapolis.

verse_quote: put his fingers into his ears.
note: These physical actions accompany the miracle of healing but are not its cause. Since the man cannot hear the spoken word, perhaps Jesus uses such signs to communicate what He intends to do for the man, inviting him to exercise faith.

A striking detail, probably reflecting an eyewitness’s recollection and perhaps expressing Jesus’ weariness and sorrow over the debilitating effects of Adam’s fall into sin that afflict all of our first parent’s descendants—the entire human race (see 8:12).

**Ephphatha.** An Aramaic word that Mark again translates for his Greek-speaking readers (5:41 note).
For the deaf, clearly expressed spoken language must usually be learned over a period of time. Instantaneous ability to articulate shows how miraculous the cure is.
Regarding Jesus’ command of secrecy, see notes on 1:34 and 5:19.

verse_quote: the deaf hear and the mute speak.
note: Is. 35:5, 6 foretold such healings as part of the Lord’s future intervention to reverse sin’s curse on His people and the earth. Jesus points to such miracles to reassure John the Baptist and his disciples that He is indeed the promised Messiah whose way John prepared (Matt. 11:2–6).
A second miraculous feeding. Jesus later points to deep theological significance in the two feedings (8:18–21).

Since this feeding probably takes place in the Decapolis (7:31), it is evident that Jesus extends His compassion from the lost sheep of the house of Israel (6:34) to the Gentiles, as His healing of the Syrophoenician woman’s daughter (7:24–30) and of a deaf and mute man in Gentile territory (7:31–37) suggest. By His actions, Jesus announces the worldwide mission of the future church.
See note on 1:4. The disciples’ question, in view of what Jesus has previously done in similar circumstances, justifies Jesus’ reproach in vv. 17, 18.

As with the feeding of the five thousand in Galilee, when Jesus offers thanks, breaks, and gives these loaves (and a few small fish), all are satisfied and seven baskets full of leftover pieces are gathered (v. 8).
Presumably on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, though its exact location is unknown (text note).

See note on 2:16.

**sign from heaven.** Jesus does not perform signs on demand, especially not for those “testing” Him (1:13; cf. Matt. 4:1–11, where the same Gk. verb is translated “tempting”). See John 6:31–34.The Pharisees want a sign to confirm that Jesus is the political messiah they are expecting (v. 15 note). Jesus’ resurrection from the dead will be the sign that confirms His identity (Matt. 12:38, 39).

This narrative detail ties this passage and the two feeding miracles together. It explains why they have misconstrued Jesus’ symbolic warning against the “leaven” of the Pharisees and Herod, fretting over a lack of physical bread when Jesus is concerned about graver spiritual dangers.

verse_quote: leaven of the Pharisees and ... Herod.
note: Jesus uses an everyday ingredient of bread as a metaphor (Luke 12:1 note). What seems like an innocent, even legitimate request for a sign (on Herod’s desire for miracles, see Luke 23:8) is actually a rejection of His ministry and all His previous signs. Jesus is warning His disciples against superficial conceptions of His role and preparing them for His teaching concerning the true meaning of His coming and of His cross (vv. 27, 31). Such teaching will remain incomprehensible to many Jews even after Jesus’ ascension (1 Cor. 1:22, 23).
The disciples’ thoughts are still dominated by material concerns, leaving them blind to the true vocation of their master and open to being tempted by the “leaven” of the Pharisees.

verse_quote: Having eyes do you not see.
note: Alarmingly, Jesus’ disciples resemble those outside His circle, to whom the secret of God’s kingdom has not been revealed (4:11, 12; Is. 6:9, 10). The questions about the disciples’ spiritual discernment in vv. 17–21, based on Is. 6:9, 10, are not declarations, as in Mark 4:12, where Jesus uses the language to describe the actual condition of the majority of unbelieving Israel. Accordingly, the disciples are part of the spiritually anesthetized lump of Israel, but they are slowly coming out of it as they continue to follow Jesus and trust in Him.

Here Jesus’ role in teaching and training the Twelve comes into the foreground of the narrative (3:14 note). His question to them is a reproach for failing to realize that the Lord who miraculously provided for five thousand men with their families and four thousand on another occasion is capable of taking care of twelve men’s physical needs. Indeed, they should know that Jesus is worthy of their total faith in all that He will reveal to them in the days to come.
A fishing town on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee and home of Philip, Andrew, and Peter.
See note on 7:33.

The restoration of sight in this case is gradual. It is surprising that it requires two steps, considering the immediate and complete healing of a deaf and mute man who was likewise brought by others and taken by Jesus to a private location for the healing. The incremental cure is not because Jesus’ healing power is limited; rather, it illustrates the condition of His disciples, who are beginning to perceive Jesus’ true identity (as Peter will confess, v. 29) yet often seem to have eyes without seeing and ears without hearing (v. 18; see also vv. 31–33).

verse_quote: Do not even enter the village.
note: Jesus led him out of the town (v. 23), so it is likely that the message of this miracle is intended for His disciples. They must realize that Jesus is gradually healing their spiritual sight. While in v. 21 they still do not understand who Jesus is, like the blind man (vv. 24, 25) they are about to see more “clearly” the mystery of His person (vv. 27–30), but not with the full clarity that they ought to have and, after the resurrection of Jesus, will have (vv. 31–33).

A town at the foot of Mount Hermon and close to the source of the Jordan River. Herod the Great built a marble temple to Caesar Augustus there, and his son Philip changed the town’s name from Paneas to Caesarea. To distinguish it from the other Caesarea, the well-known Mediterranean port, it was known as Philip’s Caesarea.

verse_quote: But who do you say that I am.
note:
Again the preeminence of the Twelve in the revelation of the person of Jesus is emphasized (v. 21; 3:14). Jesus dismisses what people say (v. 27) but acknowledges and retains as divinely revealed truth the confession of the Twelve (Matt. 16:16, 17 and notes).

**the Christ.** Lit. “the anointed one” (1 Sam. 2:10; Matt. 1:1 and notes). This is the first time in Mark’s narrative of events that the name “Christ” appears (it does appear in the title at 1:1). Peter’s confession (as spokesperson for the Twelve), along with the transfiguration that follows (9:2–13), is a high point in the revelation of Jesus’ person and a turning point in His earthly ministry. From now on His teaching will concentrate on His impending death, and He will soon begin to travel to Jerusalem.

See notes on 1:34; 5:19; see also 9:9. Strangely, at this high point of revelation comes the order to keep it secret. But with hindsight the reason is clear. Jesus will not allow political notions of messiahship to compromise His true calling as the suffering Messiah whose essentially moral and spiritual work of redemption will be total.

This section recounts the turning point of Jesus’ earthly ministry (8:29 note). It contains three predictions of Jesus’ death and resurrection (8:31; 9:31; 10:33, 34), relates the beginning of His journey to Jerusalem, and gives sustained teaching on true messiahship and discipleship.

**8:31 Son of Man.** See note on 2:10.

**must.** Behind this small word is all the weight of scriptural prophecy and divinely ordained necessity (9:31; cf. Luke 22:37; 24:7, 26, 44; Acts 1:16). Jesus’ predictions concerning His death and resurrection come out of His understanding of the OT Scriptures.

**suffer many things.** The prediction of the suffering Messiah comes particularly from Is. 52:13–53:12. See also Zech. 9:9; 12:10; 13:7; and the OT generally for the theme of the righteous sufferer. Suffering marked the lives of OT figures such as Joseph, Moses, David, and many of the prophets (12:2–5; 2 Chr. 36:15, 16).

**elders.** Lay members of the Sanhedrin, the court that governed Jewish affairs in Jesus’ day. The court was composed of elders, chief priests, and teachers of the law (the scribes).

**chief priests.** Jesus predicts that the wealthy high-priestly families who are affiliated with the Sadducees will be involved in His death.

**after three days.** See Hos. 6:2. This is also a conventional expression for a short period.

**rise again.** See Is. 52:13; 53:10; cf. Ps. 110:1; Dan. 7:13, 14. The apostles cite Ps. 16:10 to show that God would not permit His holy one to undergo corruption (Acts 2:25–32; 13:34–37).

In contrast to His public teaching in parables (4:10, 11), the Twelve privately receive plain instruction (see John 16:25, 29). Jesus’ clear, private teaching will become the basis of His disciples’ public preaching after His resurrection and outpouring of the Holy Spirit (Matt 10:27; Acts 2:29; 4:13, 29, 31; 28:31).

**Peter ... began to rebuke him.** When even Peter, leader among the Twelve, fails to accept that the Messiah must suffer, one can appreciate the wisdom of Jesus’ secrecy regarding His messianic office. Cf. Paul’s remark that for many “the word of the cross is folly” (1 Cor. 1:18; see Gal. 3:13).
Satan is now at work even among Jesus’ disciples, not only in Judas but even in Peter, whose intervention, if successful, will annul the plan of redemption and accomplish Satan’s goal.

Condemned prisoners in the first century were generally made to carry the crossbar of their cross to the site of execution (see 15:21). The suffering that awaits the Christ in Jerusalem, as He predicts to His disciples, sets the pattern for the experience of all who follow Him.

No monetary or material value can be placed on this (Ps. 49:7–9, to which Jesus is perhaps alluding). As costly as it may be to persevere as Jesus’ disciple, the consequences of shrinking back in shame are infinitely, eternally worse.

verse_quote: in the glory of his Father.
note: Though in the present time of humiliation “the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8:20), one day He will be revealed with divine splendor as the Son of God (12:6–11; 14:62; cf. Dan. 7:13; Rev. 14:14–16).

verse_quote: kingdom of God after it has come with power.
note: The coming of the kingdom “with power” seems to be associated with Jesus’ resurrection since it will be witnessed by “some standing here,” and at His resurrection Jesus is appointed “the Son of God in power” (Rom. 1:4). The exaltation that began with Christ’s resurrection included His ascension and heavenly enthronement at God’s right hand, which resulted in His outpouring of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, when His followers were “clothed with power from on high” and the evidence of the Spirit’s arrival were seen and heard by many (Luke 24:49; Acts 2:32, 33). The transfiguration, which immediately follows this utterance, may be an intermediate fulfillment of Jesus’ words, since it anticipates the manifestation of His resurrection power and divine glory. See note on Matt. 16:28.

In Ex. 24:16, “six days” is also the period of preparation for receiving revelation and witnessing a vision of divine glory (a theophany; 6:50 note).

**Peter and James and John.** These three can represent the Twelve, just as Peter alone can (8:29; Matt. 16:18; Acts 2:14). In his second epistle Peter recalls this event, when “we were eyewitnesses of his majesty” and heard God’s words acclaiming Jesus as the well-pleasing beloved Son “on the holy mountain” (2 Pet. 1:16–18).

**a high mountain.** Both Moses (on Sinai; Ex. 24) and Elijah (on Horeb; 1 Kin. 19) were given a vision of God’s theophanic presence on high mountains.

**transfigured.** Lit. “changed in form.” Paul uses this Gk. verb to describe the present work of the Spirit in the inner life of the believer (Rom. 12:2; 2 Cor. 3:18). That work will be completed when this same Spirit gives “life to your mortal bodies” as when He raised Jesus from the dead (Rom. 8:11), and as here in Jesus’ momentary glorification.

The transfiguration ties the old covenant to the new, directly linking Moses and Elijah, representatives of the law and the prophets, respectively, with Jesus and His apostles, messengers of redemption’s completion.
Peter perhaps wishes to capture and prolong the glory so as to avoid the suffering of which Jesus has already spoken (8:31–33). In any case, he speaks out of fear (v. 6).

This recalls the thick cloud that covered Mount Sinai as Moses received the law from God (Ex. 19:16; 24:15, 16) and anticipates the clouds that will accompany Jesus’ return in glory at the end of the age (14:62).

**This is my beloved Son.** The heavenly declaration is a high point of divine revelation concerning the identity of Jesus. Just as God revealed Himself in the theophany on Sinai as “the Lord, a God merciful and gracious” (Ex. 34:6), so now He reveals Himself as the one who speaks through His beloved Son (John 1:17; 3:16; Heb. 1:2). The heavenly voice echoes God’s declaration that the Messiah is “my son” (Ps. 2:7), and the earlier and similar declaration at Jesus’ baptism, affirming not only His divine identity but also His royal office.

**listen to him.** This phrase represents a rebuke to Peter as well as a declaration concerning the authority of the Son as revealer and prophet of the new covenant. These words echo Deut. 18:15 and identify Jesus as the great prophet like Moses (see Acts 3:22).

verse_quote: charged them to tell no one.
note:
See notes on 1:34; 8:30.

**until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.** Open, public testimony to Jesus’ glory is to be withheld until after the full accomplishment of redemption.

verse_quote: questioning what this rising from the dead might mean.
note: The disciples’ confusion arises from Jewish expectation of a general resurrection in the last days, but not an individual resurrection in the midst of history (since Jesus has predicted that He will rise “after three days,” 8:31).

The common expectation that Elijah will come to prepare for the messianic age occurs to the disciples because that prophet has just appeared with Moses in the transfiguration event. This expectation is based on the final prediction in the OT prophetic books (Mal. 4:5, 6). Though John the Baptist is not personally Elijah risen from the dead (6:14–16; see John 1:21), Jesus teaches that Elijah was indeed the OT type who prefigured the John’s ministry (see Luke 1:17), so John’s preparatory mission fulfilled Malachi’s prophecy.

Just as Elijah suffered at the hands of Ahab and Jezebel (1 Kin. 19:1–10), so John suffered at the hands of Herod and Herodias (6:18 note). If John, who restored all things by calling the people of God to repentance and godliness, was put to death, should it be surprising (v. 12) that the Son of Man faces the same lot?

Demon possession is clearly distinguished from normal illness (7:31–37), though in both cases the person cannot speak (cf. 1:24, 25; 5:2–15). Although the boy’s other symptoms resemble those of epilepsy (9:18, 22, 26), the evangelists distinguish suffering originating from demonic possession, as in this case, from that arising from physical causes.

Jesus’ impatience with the disciples’ lack of faith and frustration with the general scene of unbelief and impotence as He returns from the Mount of Transfiguration are reminiscent of Moses coming down from Mount Sinai to find unbelief and unfaithfulness in the Israelite camp (Ex. 32).

verse_quote: cast him into fire and into water.
note:
The evil spirits’ intention to torture and destroy their victims is again shown (5:5, 13: Rev. 9:2–6).

**if you can.** The inability of the disciples to expel the demon from his son has cast doubt in the father’s mind concerning Jesus’ power to help.

Like the Twelve, whose spiritual sight is still blurred (8:17–25), this desperate man is a mixture of faith and unbelief. Yet Jesus responds to even such fragile faith. His compassion and power bring encouragement to Mark’s readers, both in the first century and today.

The situation is still volatile. The blind enthusiasm of the crowd constantly places Jesus in the dilemma of compassionately wanting to minister to people’s suffering, while not jeopardizing the overarching plan of redemption.

**I command you.** The spiritual power of Jesus causes the demon to cry out (v. 26). See “Demons” on p. 295.
As He did to Jairus’s daughter (5:41), Jesus raises the boy by His touch.
See note on 8:32.

It is unlikely that other categories of demons can be exorcised without prayer, so Jesus probably means that this kind of being—evil spirits—cannot be driven out apart from a disciple’s humble dependence expressed in urgent prayer. The delegated authority of Jesus’ name can be exercised only through constant reliance on Jesus Himself, as the extreme case of Sceva’s sons shows (Acts 19:13–17).

Again and again Jesus gives priority to the training of the Twelve. Jesus repeats, for emphasis and because the lesson is still unlearned, the forecast of His suffering and resurrection that He previously gave them (8:31).
See note on 2:1.

The disciples’ dispute over their relative positions of honor demonstrates how thoroughly “they did not understand” Jesus’ prediction of the suffering ahead of Him (v. 32). Given the importance of honor in that society, such considerations play a significant role (see 10:35–45). Jesus is bringing about a revolution in that way of thinking, though without destroying the notion of functional hierarchy. See note on 5:37.

Again the Twelve are singled out (3:14), and their position of leadership is explicitly recognized, even as their understanding of what leadership entails is radically reconfigured.

**If anyone would be first.** Jesus is not attacking leadership positions, but showing the way in which such roles should be exercised (i.e., as the “last ... and servant of all”). This principle is exemplified by Jesus Himself, who “came not to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (10:45). The self-giving manner in which Jesus fulfills His messianic role, which is the first and foremost role in the kingdom, provides the standard for His disciples in whatever secondary roles they might exercise in the kingdom of God.

Lit. “infant.” The God-given dignity of every human being is exemplified by the little child. This weakest of human beings must be served in the same way as the greatest (9:35 note). By identifying Himself (and the Father who sent Him) with infants and toddlers, who are weak and needy rather than powerful and productive, Jesus counters the inclination to assign people’s value according to their usefulness (see 10:13–16).

This phrase does not deny that the man was a follower of Jesus; he was casting out demons in Jesus’ name. Probably what is meant is that he is not an adherent of the Twelve. Without taking away the prerogatives of the Twelve, but sensing their pride and exclusivism (9:35 note; 10:35–45), Jesus refuses to denounce the one they are talking about. Instead He teaches that the support and fellowship of all who support His cause should be gratefully acknowledged.

verse_quote: the one who is not against us is for us.
note: The effectiveness of the unnamed exorcist (in contrast to the impotence of some of the Twelve; see vv. 18, 28, 29) shows that he is using Jesus’ name in faith and by prayer even though he is not in the circle close to the Twelve. It is also true that “whoever is not with me is against me” (Matt. 12:30). In relation to Jesus there is no neutral ground.
All acts of mercy, care, and healing done in Jesus’ name (that is, with understanding and the purpose of serving Him) are eternally acknowledged as evidence of true discipleship (see Matt. 25:31–46).

“Little ones” can refer either to infants (v. 36) or to insignificant believers (v. 39). Derailing the faith of those of little worldly importance through an inconsiderate, egotistical use of power (v. 35 note) calls for the most severe punishment (v. 43).

This admonition should be understood as a kind of exaggeration used in speech to make a point (see vv. 45–47). Jesus is talking about costly and radical renunciations of sinful habits. He has already identified the fallen human heart as the origin of all defiling sins (7:20–23). See theological note “Hell” on previous page.

**9:44, 46** See text notes. Verses 44 and 46 do not appear in some early manuscripts, but the phrase also appears in v. 48. Jesus’ images of the undying worm and the unquenchable fire teach the unending torment awaiting those who die under God’s wrath, and thus the eternal significance of each individual’s response to God’s holy law and His gospel.

Salt is associated with sacrifice in Lev. 2:13; Ezek. 43:24. The saying may mean that by contrast to the fire of destruction just spoken of, believers will persevere through fire and be purified by it (1 Pet. 1:7; 4:12–19).

The image of salt describes true discipleship. Salt is a preservative. Jesus is telling His disciples to use humility and service to preserve the peace of the church rather than dividing it through a desire to be great (v. 34).
The Roman province of Judea included most of central Palestine, with Jerusalem at its center. This journey into Judea begins the process that will lead Jesus to His death (Luke 9:51).

The question is vague, because Deut. 24:1–4 already indicates that the answer depends on the circumstances. Perhaps the Pharisees want to draw Jesus into the debate about Herod Antipas and his unlawful wife (6:17 note). The two main rabbinic schools of that day disagreed on the meaning of “indecency.” The school that followed Rabbi Shammai limited this ground to sexual infidelity, whereas the school of Rabbi Hillel countenanced a wider range of reasons for a wife to “find no favor” in her husband’s eyes (Deut. 24:1). If Jesus’ questioners want Him to take sides in this debate, His conclusion is closer to Shammai’s view, but Jesus broadens the discussion by placing marriage itself in the context of God’s creational design revealed in Gen. 1:27; 2:24.

As usual, Jesus does not argue from tradition (7:1–13 note) but seeks the intention of Scripture and its real requirements (see Matt. 5:20–22, 27–32). Regarding marriage, Jesus shows that in the time of the new covenant, despite the continuing presence of sin, the creation ordinances continue to serve as norms for human life and conduct (see Eph. 5:22–33).
The creation order is to be maintained. Monogamous marriage is to be cherished and preserved.
This is a basic commandment about the inviolability of marriage. However, Jesus here specifies one valid ground for divorce—marital infidelity (Matt. 5:32; 19:9). Paul gives another (1 Cor. 7:12–16).
Lit. “infants” (9:36 note). They are young enough to be brought by their parents and taken by Jesus in His arms.

Jesus is expressing the typical OT notion of covenant solidarity. These small children belong in the kingdom, initially because of the faith of their parents, though they must exercise faith personally as soon as they can in order to inherit all the covenant blessings. God’s kingdom belongs to small children, not because they are innocent but because they model true believers who have nothing to bring and everything to receive (v. 15).
To receive God’s blessing means to be called by God’s name (Gen. 48:16; Num. 6:22–27) and to be included in the blessings of the covenant (Gen. 22:16–18; Deut. 7:13).

This man has great wealth (v. 22), is a ruler (Luke 18:18), and is young (Matt. 19:22). He has everything and yet lacks the most important thing—eternal life.

**what must I do to inherit.** The two verbs “do” and “inherit” placed together, the list of moral achievements, and the young man’s understanding of goodness (v. 18 note) indicate a religious outlook based on works righteousness.

verse_quote: Why do you call me good.
note: Jesus’ reply does not mean that He does not consider Himself good. He rather wants to show the man that “no one is good except God alone” so that the man may realize that all his works do not make him good and that he is not capable of earning eternal life.

This prohibition, virtually synonymous with “do not steal,” comes where the order of the Ten Commandments leads us to expect, “Do not covet” (Ex. 20:13–17). Perhaps Jesus substitutes this term (which, like stealing and coveting, pertains to possessions) in order to defer momentarily the issue of the rich man’s heart allegiance (which, if he were honest, should be exposed by “do not covet”), in anticipation of Jesus’ climactic and crucial ultimatum: “Sell all that you have.”

Jesus’ final demand springs from a heartfelt desire to see this man set free from the illusion of self-righteousness and from captivity to his property.

**You lack one thing.** The young man’s love of riches (v. 22) and refusal to give them up to follow Jesus shows that he has broken the greatest commandment of all: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (Deut. 6:5; see Matt. 22:37). Lacking the total righteousness that God requires, he stands condemned.

verse_quote: How difficult it will be for those who have wealth.
note: The difficulty is not because riches are evil and disqualify those who possess them, but because the rich are tempted to depend upon their riches for their security, leaving it hard for many of them to admit their need of God (see 1 Tim. 6:9, 17).

An excellent example of Jesus’ colorful, hyperbolic language, here expressing the idea of impossibility (v. 27). The suggestion that there was a small gate in ancient Judea, called “the needle’s eye,” through which camels could barely pass is unsupported and trivializes Jesus’ illustration.

A simplistic reading of the covenant blessings and curses in the law of Moses (Deut. 28) and other OT texts fostered a widespread assumption that material wealth was an indication of God’s pleasure. Apparently, the disciples have inferred that if the rich could not be saved, salvation is out of the question for those less affluent.

Salvation is beyond the reach of human achievement for rich and for poor. It is from the Lord, through sovereign, divine initiative (Ps. 3:8; 68:19, 20), not by human effort (Eph. 2:8, 9). He can achieve what is humanly impossible (Gen. 18:14; Luke 1:37).
While salvation cannot be earned, allegiance to Christ entails surrendering to Him control of one’s life, including possessions and relationships.

The phrase “this time” with its counterpart “the age to come” reflects the teaching of the rabbis about the two-tiered present evil age and the future age of the Messiah. The resurrection of Jesus significantly alters that view. In the period between the resurrection of Jesus and that of all believers the “two ages” exist in overlap. The old is passing away, and the new is present but not in its fullness. Hence there can be both a “hundredfold” blessing and “persecution.” Through God’s providence, the Spirit’s presence, and the global church as the family of God, disciples’ needs are met even in the present age, so that in Christ they can be content in every situation, whether in abundance or in need (Phil. 4:11–13).

verse_quote: Son of Man will be delivered.
note:
See note on 8:31.

**Gentiles.** The new element in this third prediction of the passion is the mention of the Gentiles (i.e., the Romans). The flogging and mockery He predicts are details of His death prophesied in the Scriptures (Ps. 22:7; Is. 50:6; 53:5), and were normal Roman practice.

See 1:19 and 3:17.
