Again Jesus’ prediction of His coming humiliation and suffering is followed immediately by His disciples’ quest for prominence, which stands in starkest contrast to His humility (see 9:30–35). They still do not understand but are gripped with amazement and fear (10:32). In Matt. 20:20 it is their mother who makes the request, so apparently the whole family is involved.
Jesus’ teaching on greatness (9:34, 35 and notes) clearly has yet to change their attitudes.

An OT symbol for suffering and wrath (Ps. 75:8; Is. 51:17–22; Jer. 25:15; Ezek. 23:31–34).

**baptism.** Here the word is a metaphor for the experience of death-threatening judgment, with the hope of ultimate deliverance (Rom. 6:3–7; 1 Cor. 10:2; Col. 2:11–13). The floodwaters of Noah’s day and the drowning of Egypt’s forces at the exodus reinforced the imagery of water as symbolizing divinely imposed destruction (Ps. 43:7; 69:1, 2).

Though Zebedee’s sons are naively overconfident in their present ability to endure suffering (see 14:50), they will share their Lord’s sufferings in the future—not contributing to His unique mission of atonement, but paying a painful price to proclaim the message of His cross (Phil. 3:10; Col. 1:24) and following the example of His own suffering (1 Pet. 2:20–23).
Jesus recognizes areas where only the Father has authority (13:32). His humble submission is a rebuke to His disciples’ self-centered ambition.

Perhaps the others are indignant not because John and James have failed to put Jesus’ teaching into practice (9:35 note), but because they want the same high places. Jesus desires to eliminate such notions of power and authority in the Twelve and, by extension, in all His disciples.

verse_quote: the Son of Man came not to be served.
note:
To correct His disciples’ worldly understanding of power and authority, Jesus presents them with His own example. Jesus, the Son of Man who will inherit “dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples ... should serve him” (Dan. 7:14), has come first as a suffering servant, fulfilling the prophecy of Is. 52:13–53:12. In first serving others, Jesus has begun to inaugurate the Dan. 7:13, 14 kingdom, which will result in others serving Him.

**ransom.** A price paid to free the guilty from a sentence (Ex. 21:30) or debtors from their debt (Ex. 30:12; see Is. 53:10).

**many.** See Is. 53:12. In the Qumran writings (the Dead Sea Scrolls), this is a term for all the members of the community. When instituting the Lord’s Supper, Jesus identifies the cup with His blood, “poured out for many” (14:24).

Fifteen miles (24 km) northeast of Jerusalem and eight hundred feet (244 m) below sea level. See note on Luke 18:35.

**Bartimaeus ... the son of Timaeus.** The translation shows that Mark is writing for an audience unfamiliar with Semitic languages (5:41 note). Mark alone preserves this identification, yet the translation implies that the blind beggar’s personal name is unknown to the uncaring crowd of passersby, who refer to him only in terms of his father.
A popular messianic title (11:10; 12:35) drawn from the OT (Is. 11:1–3; Jer. 23:5, 6; Ezek. 34:23, 24).
One of the marks of Jesus’ public ministry is the time He gives to suffering individuals in the midst of crowds (5:30–34).

verse_quote: What do you want me to do for you.
note: Although others have tried to silence the beggar as an annoying nuisance, Jesus the servant asks him the same question He asked James and John, two of His closest disciples (v. 36).

verse_quote: when they drew near to Jerusalem.
note:
The journey (10:1 note) reaches its destination, and what is called “Passion Week” begins. Jesus’ decision to come up to Jerusalem is clearly determined by His understanding of the OT and His prophecies concerning His death (8:31 note).

**Bethphage and Bethany.** Villages just east of Jerusalem.

**Mount of Olives.** East of Jerusalem and rising about two hundred feet (61 m) higher than the Temple Mount, this high hill commands a spectacular view of Jerusalem and especially of the temple. In Jesus’ time it was covered with olive trees, but was stripped of them by the Romans during the siege of Jerusalem in A.D. 70.

This text may witness to the supernatural knowledge of Jesus (see John 1:48–50).

**colt.** A young donkey (Matt. 21:2; John 12:15). Matthew and John note that the OT prophesied Jesus’ actions (Zech. 9:9), which identify Him clearly as the righteous messianic King, coming humbly to bring salvation to Jerusalem (Matt. 21:5; John 12:14, 15).
A recognition of Jesus’ royal dignity (see 2 Kin. 9:12, 13).

A Gk. transliteration of the Aramaic words for “Save us ... O Lord” (Ps. 118:25). The crowd is shouting phrases from that psalm, which celebrates the procession of the royal Messiah.

**he who comes in the name of the Lord.** This description of the Messiah from Ps. 118:26 echoes David’s self-description in his confrontation with Goliath (1 Sam. 17:45).

verse_quote: the coming kingdom of our father David.
note: The crowd expects that Jesus’ arrival marks the beginning of a military-political insurgency that will banish Roman forces from the Promised Land.

In Matt. 21:12–22 Jesus proceeds to cleanse the temple upon His arrival and curses the fig tree the next day (cf. Luke 19:45, 46). In Mark, Jesus returns to Bethany for the night; in the morning He curses the fig tree and then cleanses the temple. Probably Matthew treats the material topically (no specific time reference for the cleansing is given in Matt. 21:12), while Mark, who places stories within stories (5:21–43; 6:7–30), treats it chronologically.

verse_quote: May no one ever eat fruit from you again.
note: Jesus curses the fig tree as a miraculous prophetic sign that God will soon destroy Jerusalem and its temple (which He is about to purge of defiling business dealings) in judgment on Israel’s spiritual fruitlessness (13:2), climaxing in the rejection of the Messiah within the week. This prophetic sign indicates that the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem will no longer be a goal of redemptive history. Speaking through the prophet Jeremiah, God compared Israel’s unfaithfulness to a fig tree that bears no figs and to inedible figs that will thrown away as garbage (Jer. 8:13; 24:1–10).

That is, the Gentile court, the outermost court in the complex of structures surrounding the temple proper. It is the only area where Gentiles are allowed in Jesus’ day (see v. 17).

**began to drive out.** John 2:12–22 describes the temple cleansing at the beginning of Jesus’ ministry, while all three Synoptic Gospels report one occurring at the end. It is likely that Jesus cleanses the temple twice. John’s account is carefully dated (John 2:20; Mark 1:9 note), and the accounts are by no means identical. In John, Jesus comes with His disciples, and His actions recall to their minds Ps. 69:9. In the Synoptic accounts Jesus comes in triumphal messianic glory and justifies His actions by quoting Is. 56:7 and Jer. 7:11. Jesus is no doubt aware that the prophet Jeremiah twice cursed the temple (Jer. 7:1–15; 26:2–6).

**money-changers.** This service is necessary because the temple tax and offerings must be paid in the currency that did not bear the emperor’s image, but the service has become so corrupt that Jesus describes the scene as “a den of robbers” (v. 17; Luke 19:45, 46 note). Jesus is also judging the Sadducean high-priestly families who are not honoring the character of the Father whose house it is (see 12:18–27).

verse_quote: not allow anyone to carry anything.
note: Not only has the court become a market, but it is being used as a shortcut by merchants of all kinds. Mark sees in Jesus’ gesture a defense of Gentile access to God in the temple and an indication of the future mission to the Gentiles.

Mark alone includes these words in Jesus’ citation of Is. 56:7. Since money changing and the sale of sacrificial animals takes place in the court of the Gentiles, it is particularly distracting to non-Jews who come to worship the God of Israel. Again Mark records Jesus’ purpose to include all nations in God’s covenant community, anticipating the multiethnic composition of the church after Pentecost.

Jesus knowingly acts under the eyes of those who will kill Him (8:31).

**astonished at his teaching.** As in 1:22 and throughout His ministry, Jesus’ teaching amazes hearers both for its unique authority and for its distinctive content as announcing the arrival of God’s eschatological reign.
This phrase indicates complete destruction (v. 14 note).

verse_quote: Be taken up and thrown into the sea.
note: Jesus again uses hyperbole to emphasize the importance of confident faith in God’s power and willingness to respond to His children’s prayer.

Believing prayer brings one into God’s holy presence, exposing our need for His forgiveness, a need that obligates us to forgive others (Matt. 6:12, 14, 15; 18:23–35) and to seek their forgiveness for sins we have committed against them (Matt. 5:23, 24).

**11:26** This verse is lacking in certain ancient manuscripts (text note). A similar saying is found in Matt. 6:15.

The chief priests of the Sadducean party, which control the administration of the temple, along with the elders and scribes, challenge Jesus’ authority to purge the court of the Gentiles of the business enterprises that serve the convenience of pilgrims coming to worship, while filling temple coffers. He has no official standing in the Sanhedrin, so these authorities want to know how He can dare to take such action.

Jesus’ response silences the officeholders and professional theologians, for it undercuts the claims of such official authority to be absolute. Prophetic authority cannot, by definition, have a human source (Gal. 1:11, 12). It is attested by God and demands submission. Implied in Jesus’ question, which they decline to answer, is an _unspoken_ and ultimate question: “Do you recognize and submit to My authority?”

Jesus refuses to affirm explicitly His divine authority to those who avoid affirming John’s prophetic call from God. Yet the parable of the tenants, which He is about to tell, identifies Him implicitly as God’s Son, whose arrival and mistreatment by Israel’s leaders climax the history of the nation’s response to God’s messengers.

This pronoun apparently refers to the chief priests and scribes since it agrees with “they” in v. 12 (those who look for a way to arrest Him).

**parables.** See notes on 4:2, 11. Although it is incorrect to seek a special, symbolic meaning for every detail of the parable, the essential point is clear.

**vineyard.** The parable is based on the “Song of the Vineyard” (Is. 5:1–5), which pictures Israel and her unfaithfulness. Also, in Is. 3:14 the Lord rebukes Israel’s leaders (elders and princes) for exploiting His vineyard.

Often a term for the prophets (Ex. 14:31; 2 Chr. 1:3; Is. 20:3; Amos 3:7), whom Jesus sees as those God sent to call Israel to faithfulness and who often suffered death (Matt. 23:37). The sending of a succession of servants to collect fruit as rent recasts in the parable’s fictional narrative the history of Israel’s mistreatment of God’s prophets (cf. 2 Chr. 36:15, 16).

**tenants.** Those with official authority over the people of God, particularly those for whom the parable is told. By casting them as renters in the story, Jesus reminds them that Israel belongs to God, to whom they are accountable.

The theme of Jesus as God’s beloved Son is rare and voiced at critical junctures in Mark’s gospel (1:11, 9:7), but it is unmistakably present. In the parable, the son clearly outranks both the tenants and the servants who preceded him to lay claim to what is due the owner.

Matt. 21:43 reads that the vineyard “will be ... given to a people producing its fruits,” suggesting both the community of disciples forming around Jesus, now led by the apostles (Luke 22:29, 30), and the eventual mission to the Gentiles (Matt. 8:11, 12; Rom. 9:22–26).

verse_quote: The stone that the builders rejected.
note: Jesus cites Ps. 118:22, 23. That psalm, the source of the crowd’s recent praises on Palm Sunday (11:9), celebrates the victory that God gives to His Messiah, establishing Him on His throne. The psalm’s architectural imagery especially alludes to the temple and shows that Jesus is identified with the reestablishment of the temple, thus representing the very presence of God that has been sequestered in the back room of the temple for so long. That the “rejected stone” has “become the cornerstone” of the new temple suggests that God will reverse human leaders’ negative assessment of the Messiah, and this is fulfilled in Jesus’ condemnation to death by the Sanhedrin and subsequent resurrection. Such is the confidence of Jesus in His Father and in the Scriptures that He can rejoice in the promised victory even in the face of the death He has just predicted for Himself (“they took him and killed him”; v. 8).
Although the meaning of other parables is usually hidden from those outside Jesus’ circle (4:11, 12), the import of this one is obvious to His enemies.

verse_quote: Pharisees and some of the Herodians.
note: The alliance between the Pharisees and the Herodians reemerges (3:6). This alliance is possible because both parties accept the Roman occupation, the former as a divine punishment on the sins of the Jews, the latter for political advantage.

In addition to numerous customs taxes, tolls, and other charges (2:14 note), each Roman province was obliged to pay the imperial tribute. The same sum was exacted from all, rich and poor alike. This tax was unpopular with the people.

verse_quote: Why put me to the test.
note:
His opponents’ question is apparently an attempt to brand Jesus as a political revolutionary or as complicit in Rome’s occupation of God’s land and oppression of God’s people.

**denarius.** Numerous currencies were in circulation in Palestine during the first century. Jesus asks for the Roman denarius, about a day’s wage, bearing on one side a picture of Caesar and on the other a scene glorifying his reign.

Jesus takes the occasion to affirm that Rome’s political power is legitimate, as at His trial He declares that it is from God (John 19:11). The early church followed this teaching of Jesus (Rom. 13:1–7; Col. 1:16; 1 Tim. 2:1–6; Titus 3:1, 2; 1 Pet. 2:13–17).

**to God the things that are God’s.** Governments have legitimate claims on their subjects by God’s appointment, but their domain is not universal. Since the “likeness” on the denarius (v. 16) is the Gk. word rendered “image” in Gen. 1:26, describing the creation of human beings in the “image of God,” Jesus may be challenging His questioners to devote themselves wholly to the God whose image they bear.

The Sadducees denied the resurrection and the existence of angels, and they rejected the oral tradition of the Pharisees (Acts 23:8). Their name probably derives from Zadok, David’s high priest (2 Sam. 8:17; 1 Chr. 15:11; 29:22) and appointed officer over the Aaronic priestly line (1 Chr. 27:17) who was given the exclusive right to be high priest (Ezek. 40:46; 43:19).

The story they tell Jesus (vv. 19–23) is based on the “kinsman-redeemer” (or “levirate [brother-in-law] marriage”) commandment of Deut. 25:5–10, which provides for a family line to be perpetuated by the nearest of kin in the event of a premature death (Ruth 2:20 note).

That is, the implications of God’s self-identification to Moses in Ex. 3, which Jesus is about to cite.

**nor the power of God.** Probably refers to God’s power to bring about, through His Messiah, a completely new order of existence in the new heavens and the new earth at the end of time (Luke 22:69; Rom. 1:16; 1 Cor. 1:18, 24).

The final resurrection marks the complete transformation of the physical universe (Rom. 8:21; 1 Cor. 15:52, 53). Therefore, the creation mandate of marriage and reproduction (Gen. 1:27, 28; 2:24), which applies to human relationships in the present order, will no longer be needed or appropriate.

See Ex. 3:1–6. The God who appears with miraculous power in the theophany of the burning bush is the Lord not of “the dead” but of the “living,” those who are united to Him in an eternal covenant of grace. Although the patriarchs had been in the grave for centuries when the Lord spoke to Moses, by identifying Himself as their God He affirmed His commitment to redeem them as whole persons, body and soul, for communion with Himself. The teaching about resurrection, Jesus implies, is not limited to certain OT proof texts (e.g., Job 19:25–27; Ps. 16:9–11; 17:15; 73:24–26; Is. 26:19; 53:11; Ezek. 37:1–14; Dan. 12:2; Hos. 6:2; 13:14) but is grounded in the person of the living and life-giving God.
This strong phrase recalls Jesus’ damning indictment of those who adamantly resist God’s truth despite their learning and positions of religious influence.

verse_quote: seeing that he answered them well.
note: This scribe’s responses may show that his question is sincere, not a trick or a test.

Jesus joins Lev. 19:18 to Deut. 6:4, 5, a text that James calls “the royal law” (James 2:8).
The scribe approves Jesus’ answer and adds a scriptural proof of his own (1 Sam. 15:22; Ps. 40:6; Hos. 6:6).

The scribe’s reply indicates that his heart is not as hard as those of his colleagues. Compare the rich young ruler of 10:21 (“You lack one thing”) and Nicodemus (John 3:1–21). In each case there is a need for new birth into eternal life (entering the kingdom of God), something made possible by the death and resurrection of the Son of Man (John 3:3, 14, 15).
Having silenced His interrogators, Jesus goes on the offensive with His own question about Scripture’s testimony to the identity of the Messiah.

Jesus’ interpretation hangs on the Davidic authorship of this psalm.

Ordinarily sons are considered subordinate to their fathers and earlier ancestors. Jesus argues that while the Messiah is descended from David, His royal dignity and power far surpass the royal power and dignity of David, for David addressed this coming King as “my Lord” (Ps. 110:1). This king is uniquely associated with the Lord and identified as Lord (Ps. 110:2). The crowds hear such clear and faithful interpretation of Scripture “gladly” (see Luke 24:32), although it no doubt frustrates and further enrages their leaders.

The superficiality of the scribes’ messianic doctrine and exegesis brings Jesus to criticize their hypocritical lifestyle in general. Their blend of religious showiness with exploitation of widows sets a dangerous example. A similar warning appears in 8:15.

It was considered improper for anyone to receive a salary for interpreting the Scriptures in the first century. Consequently, they relied upon and sometimes took advantage of the hospitality of the people, among whom pious widows were especially vulnerable.

**long prayers.** See Matt. 6:5, 6 for a similar judgment of ostentatious and hypocritical spirituality.
The offering boxes are situated in the women’s court of the temple, which gives access to all.

This coin, the lepton, was the lowest denomination in circulation.

**a penny.** A Roman coin worth one sixty-fourth of a denarius (the denarius was one day’s wage). Mark calculates the two coins’ value using a Gk. loanword from Latin for readers in Rome (5:41 note).
Her willingness to give sacrificially, despite her poverty, makes her gift of greater value to God than larger donations from the affluent (cf. 2 Cor. 8:1–5, 12).

This chapter is known as the “Little Apocalypse” or the Olivet Discourse. It makes predictions in three areas: the coming destruction of the temple and signs preceding it (vv. 1–4, 14–31); future persecution and deception that will generally characterize the present age (vv. 5–13); and the end of the age (vv. 32–37).

**13:1 what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings.** Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple in 19 B.C., using marble and gold as decorative materials. The outer court measured 500 by 300 yards (457 m by 274 m). It was bordered by walls of massive white stones, some of which were sixteen feet long (5 m) and three to four feet high (1 m). On top of these were magnificent, covered cloisters or walkways with richly carved wooden ceilings.
Jerusalem was sacked and the temple burned and destroyed in A.D. 70 by Titus, the Roman general (later emperor). The Arch of Titus commemorating his victory still stands in Rome.

verse_quote: Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately.
note: This teaching is part of the special instruction given to the Twelve (4:10, 11; 8:29).

The disciples’ question has in view the predicted destruction of the temple. In Matt. 24:3 the form of their question suggests that they associated that catastrophe with Jesus’ coming at the end of the age. However, Jesus’ reply addresses both the temple’s destruction within that generation’s lifetime (v. 30) and the (more distant) time leading to the end of the age, thereby separating the temple’s destruction from His second coming. The events surrounding the destruction of the temple anticipate and typify those associated with the second coming, although the former will be preceded by observable signs (13:14–31) whereas the timing of Christ’s return is known only to the Father (13:32–36).

Acts 5:36, 37; 21:38; and the Jewish historian Josephus mention first-century insurrectionists (Theudas, Judas the Galilean, an Egyptian) who claimed a special calling from God to liberate the Jewish people from Rome. Jesus forewarns His disciples that others like them will arise in the next forty years, before Jerusalem’s fall in A.D. 70, and cautions them not to mistake them for Himself, the true Messiah. Later, in A.D. 130, Bar Kochba, the leader of a Jewish rebellion against the Romans, claimed to be and was accepted by his followers as the messiah, and the list of false messiahs has only grown longer since then.

**I am he.** This phrase is also the name of God (Ex. 3:14) and the title chosen by Jesus (Mark 6:50; John 8:28, 58).

According to the parallel text (Matt. 24:3), “the end” is “the close of the age.” Neither the appearance of religious imposters nor the escalation of international conflict signifies that the end of the present age is imminent.
First-century Jews expected a time of suffering before the coming of the Messiah and described it in this way, as does Paul in Rom. 8:22.

Synagogue councils in this era have the right to order floggings, limited to forty strokes (Deut. 25:1–3). The apostles later suffer imprisonments and floggings (Acts 4:21; 5:18, 40; 2 Cor. 6:9; 11:23, 24).

The time between Christ’s resurrection and His second coming is not simply a time of suffering and persecution. It is also a time of grace and of evangelism throughout the earth in fulfillment of the prophecy of Is. 49:6.

This is a promise of special assistance in time of need rather than a reference to the ministry of the Spirit among the Twelve in establishing their proclamation of Jesus (John 14:25, 26; 15:26, 27; 16:12–15).

See note on v. 7. This statement may also mean the end of each person’s life. Such perseverance is often associated with suffering (Rom. 8:18–25; 12:12; Heb. 10:32; 12:2; 1 Pet. 2:20).

**will be saved.** Such steadfastness does not merit salvation but is the proof that true salvation has been received and can never be interrupted for the believer (Rom. 8:24).

Dan. 11:31 predicts the coming of the king of the north who will desecrate the temple. That prediction was first fulfilled in 168 B.C., when Antiochus IV Epiph­anes set up a pagan altar and sacrificed a pig in the Most Holy Place. In A.D. 70 the OT text was definitively fulfilled when Titus, the Roman general, sacked the temple.

**let the reader understand.** This phrase is either an aside by Mark for his readers or Jesus’ wish that His hearers, as readers of the OT, will realize that He is citing Dan. 9:25–27 and 11:31 (see 2:25; 12:10, 26).

**flee to the mountains.** When the Romans on their way to Jerusalem in A.D. 69 sacked Qumran, the members of that community hid their manuscripts in mountain caves overlooking the Dead Sea. Eusebius, the fourth-century church historian, states that the Christians left Jerusalem at that time and founded the church at Pella, east of the Jordan and forty to fifty miles (80 km) north of Jerusalem.

The Roman historian Tacitus and the Jewish historian Josephus describe the destruction of the temple as a catastrophe of supernatural dimensions, with armies appearing in the sky and a supernatural voice. According to Josephus, the suffering was unparalleled.

This probably refers to the limited period surrounding the destruction of the temple, but the brevity of that horrific period provides a preview of a similar period before the second coming (v. 4 note; see Rev. 20:4, 7–9).

**the sake of the elect.** The people of God (vv. 22, 27).
See note on v. 6.
Jesus associates these with messianic manifestations, though He recognizes such manifestations to be fraudulent.

Since this is a technical OT term for the last days (Jer. 3:16; Joel 3:1; Zech. 8:23), Jesus may be starting to speak of the end (see v. 7). According to some interpreters, the second coming is in view in v. 26.

**the sun will be darkened.** Although these phrases often refer to the time of God’s cosmic and final judgment (Is. 13:10; 34:4; Joel 2:10, 31), here they may signify another event so momentous that after it the world will never be the same again. Peter interprets Joel 2:31 in Acts 2:16–21 as a prophecy of the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost.

In Scripture, clouds sometimes signify divine presence (Ex. 19:9; 24:15–18). If the first coming of the Son of Man is characterized by suffering and humiliation (8:31 note), His future coming at the end will be an open declaration of His divine glory. Such a coming recalls the visible manifestations of God (theophanies) in the OT (Ex. 19:16; 34:5; Ezek. 1:4; 10:3, 4), with the difference that this one will be universal. But Dan. 7:13, 14, the source of Jesus’ imagery here, is a scene of His ascension in which the Son of Man comes with clouds into God’s heavenly court to receive eternal and universal dominion. Thus it is possible that vv. 24–27 may point not only to Christ’s appearance in universal judgment but also to humans’ realization that Jesus is reigning in the kingdom of God (Dan. 7:13)—a realization triggered by the fall of Jerusalem (God’s final judgment on the city) and by the gathering of God’s elect from the nations through evangelism. Verse 27 would then refer to the worldwide spread of the gospel that preceded and followed that event. The “angels” would be the messengers of the gospel (_angelos_ is the Gk. word for “messenger,” either human or angelic). On this view, Jesus’ first exclusive reference to the end (His second coming) is not until v. 32 (“that day”).
A poetic way of affirming the universality of the new people of God.

There does not seem to be any specific symbolic sense to this “fig tree” (such as the reemergence of the nation of Israel), especially since the parallel passage (Luke 21:29) adds “and all the trees,” although the fig tree that Jesus recently cursed symbolizes the impending rejection of unbelieving Israel and its institutions (Mark 11:12–14). Just as there are signs of what is to come in the natural realm, so there are signs of what is to come in the spiritual realm.
Concerning the destruction of the temple, the phrase refers to Jesus’ own generation.

verse_quote: Heaven and earth will pass away.
note: Jesus makes His words equal to the words of Scripture, with eternal value (see Matt. 5:18).

Jesus is conscious of His unique relationship to the Father as the eternal Son, yet with respect to His true human nature there is a limitation of His knowledge. According to Jesus’ humanity, what the Father has not revealed to Him about the future He does not know.

verse_quote: you do not know when the time will come.
note: Unlike the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple, the end of the age at Jesus’ bodily second coming will not be predictable by clearly observable signs (Acts 1:7). Also, Mark 13:1–30 repeatedly speaks of “those days” or merely the “days” relating to circumstances concerning the fall of Jerusalem that the disciples can know about, whereas v. 32 refers to that “day or that hour” (singular) that “no one knows,” likely referring to the very end of history at Christ’s final coming. The certainty of Christ’s return and uncertainty as to its timing provide the strongest motivation to stay awake and be found faithful at His arrival.

That is, Passover would be “on the second (or next) day;” cf. 8:31. Mark places the plotting of the chief priests and scribes on Wednesday of Passion Week.

**the Passover.** The Passover is one of the most important of the Jewish feasts, since it celebrates the deliverance from Egypt when the angel of death “passed over” the homes of the people of Israel (Ex. 12:1–30). At the time of Jesus, the Passover was celebrated on the fourteenth day of the first month of the Jewish calendar (Nisan,which corresponds to the end of March and beginning of April). It was observed the last day before the first full moon after the spring equinox. On that day when the paschal lambs were killed and eaten, all leaven (symbolizing sin) was to be removed from the house, and only unleavened bread was to be eaten for the seven days after the Passover. The entire eight-day observance, beginning with Passover evening, was inclusively called the “Feast of Unleavened Bread” (14:12; Ex. 12:15–20).

**chief priests.** See note on 8:31.

**scribes.** See note on 7:1.

Being one of the Jewish pilgrimage feasts, the Passover drew enormous numbers of people to Jerusalem. Josephus estimated that the population of 50,000 increased to 3,000,000. Though his figures are generally considered greatly exaggerated (250,000 is more likely), the authorities’ fears are not groundless. See 11:8–10, 31, 32; 12:12, 37.

See note on 11:1.

**Simon the leper.** No doubt no longer a leper, he may have been cleansed by Jesus. He is clearly an important member of the wider circle of disciples, since Jesus chooses to visit his house at this time.

**reclining.** For formal dinners in first-century Judea, people reclined rather than sat at the table (Luke 22:14 note; John 13:23).

**a woman.** According to John 12:3, this woman is Mary, the sister of Lazarus and Martha. John also indicates that the meal occurs “six days before the Passover” (John 12:1), before Jesus entered Jerusalem. Mark may have placed the account here to associate this pre-anointing for burial (v. 8 note) more closely with the plot to kill Jesus (v. 1). Matthew agrees with Mark’s order (Matt. 26:3–13).

**alabaster flask.** Alabaster is a type of gypsum, in its pure form white or translucent, found in limestone deposits in caves and at the exits of springs. It was often used for making ointment jars and was considered a luxury item.

**pure nard.** A rare and costly perfume imported from India and made from the root of a plant grown in the Himalayas. Its value of “three hundred denarii” (v. 5) is roughly equivalent to a year’s wages in the first century.

**broke the flask.** To prevent loss, amounts suitable for a single application were sealed into flasks that were then broken at the neck at the time of use. According to John 12:3, Mary’s flask contains twelve ounces of perfume.

Jesus commends ongoing generosity to the poor, but devotion to Him, while He is still among His disciples, takes precedence (v. 7). John notes that Judas Iscariot is among the objectors to the “waste” of this precious ointment, and that his motive is not compassion for the poor but personal greed (John 12:4–6).

Jesus approves of what others see as a waste, for by this gesture she shows the inestimable worth of Jesus, of His death (v. 8), and of the profound communion that His sacrifice on the cross will establish. This gesture recalls the precious ointment poured over Aaron the high priest, which the psalmist compares to the priceless blessing of the fellowship of believers (Ps. 133).

verse_quote: anointed my body beforehand for burial.
note: Jesus alludes to the anointing of dead bodies with spices and perfume, a common first-century practice in Palestine. His resurrection from the dead will prevent other women from performing this act of devoted love after his burial (16:1).

Judas stands in stark contrast to the unnamed woman (in Mark) who has lavished costly love on Jesus. Judas will receive thirty silver coins (not even half the value of the perfume) for his betrayal of Jesus (v. 11).

This feast symbolizes the removal of sin in the lives of Israelite believers (Ex. 12:14–20). The Passover meal falls on the first day of this feast (v. 1 note; Ex. 12:14, 15), the fourteenth day after the beginning of the Jewish year (Ex. 12:6).

**sacrificed the Passover lamb.** Jesus died at Passover, the feast that celebrates how the blood of a lamb protected the Israelites in Egypt from God’s wrath. Jesus’ death shows the profound continuity in the divine plan of redemption (see 1 Cor. 5:7). In the order of these feasts, the priority of God’s act of salvation (Passover and redemption) is shown to precede our response of holy living (Feast of Unleavened Bread and the believer’s putting away of sin).

verse_quote: man carrying a jar of water.
note: Women usually carried water jars in Jesus’ day. For Jesus’ knowledge of future and distant events, see 11:1, 2 and John 1:48. As the incarnate God-man in whose one person His fully divine nature and fully human nature are united, Jesus can and does exercise on earth divine powers of knowledge (13:32 note). It is possible, however, that Jesus has simply made prior arrangements with this man.

The Gospels record that those present at this high point in the ministry of Jesus are the twelve disciples He chose at the beginning (see 3:14). According to Luke 22:30, at this time Jesus announces their future ministry as judges of the new people of God. They are witnesses at the inauguration of the new covenant.

Jesus’ prediction of the betrayal comes from His intimate knowledge of Judas and also from His understanding of the Scriptures (v. 21; Ps. 41:9; see Acts 1:15–20).

**dipping bread into the dish with me.** Bread or meat was dipped into a central bowl of sauce. The detail emphasizes the deep personal betrayal, since table fellowship is a token of genuine friendship (see 2:16).

See note on 8:31.

**woe to that man.** Although Judas’s betrayal is part of God’s plan and predicted in Scripture, his motives and treachery are not thereby excused. His subsequent suicide is symptomatic of the eternal condemnation he incurs.

The sacramental meal of the new covenant is intrinsically related to and grows out of that of the old (cf. Ex. 24:9–11). Jesus takes two elements of the Passover meal, unleavened bread and wine, to express His new work of redemption. See “The Lord’s Supper” at 1 Cor. 11:23.

In the original Passover the blood of the lamb protected the Israelites from death (Ex. 12:23, 30). The phrase “blood of the covenant” comes from Ex. 24:8 and recalls that biblical covenants are sealed in blood, which symbolizes the lethal consequences of violating the covenant commitment (Gen. 15:9–21; 17:9–14; Ex. 24:4–8; Heb. 9:15). As in Moses’s day, divine judgment will pass over those who are covered by the blood of the final Passover lamb, Jesus Christ.

**poured out for many.** Jesus is alluding to Is. 53:12, where the servant of the Lord “poured out His soul to death” and “bore the sin of many.”

Jesus is hereby predicting the imminence of His death.

**drink it new.** Jesus expresses His faith in God, who will not abandon Him in death.

**the kingdom of God.** The eschatological reign of God, foretold by the OT prophets and announced as “at hand” by John the Baptist and Jesus (1:15; Matt. 3:1, 2), was inaugurated in Jesus’ ministry and is about to reach a greater stage in Jesus’ sacrifice and resurrection (Acts 2:30–36).
This mention of singing may refer to the Passover liturgy. If so, Jesus and His disciples sing Pss. 115–118, the Hallel of Egypt, which is the traditional close of the meal.
Not only Jesus’ suffering but also the fact that His disciples will abandon Him is predicted in ancient Scripture (Zech. 13:7).
The angel at the empty tomb will recall this promise and allude to Peter’s denial (16:7).
For other examples of Jesus’ knowledge of future events, see note on v. 13. The seemingly specific reference could also be a poetic way of saying “before dawn.”

verse_quote: If I must die with you.
note: Jesus’ followers must carry the cross, an instrument of death, and be willing to lose their lives for His sake, unashamed to identify with Him (8:34). Peter believes that he has such strong faith, but he is mistaken (vv. 66–72).

As in the display of His glory at the transfiguration, so now in the depth of His struggle with the prospect of the suffering that awaits in His Father’s will, Jesus seeks the company of these three closest disciples. See note on 5:37.

**troubled.** This verb expresses deep emotional distress (Phil. 2:26).

A colloquial Aramaic word for “father,” which expresses Jesus’ close relationship with God the Father. Mark records the Semitic word used by Jesus along with its Gk. equivalent for his readers’ comprehension, as he does elsewhere (5:41; 7:34; 11:9; 14:45; 15:22, 34). Perhaps alluding to the tradition of Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane, Paul declares that by the Spirit believers may address God as “Abba Father” (Gal. 4:6; Rom. 8:15).

**cup.** As in OT imagery, the cup symbolizes God’s wrath and the destruction it inflicts (Is. 51:17–22). See note on 10:38.

**not what I will, but what you will.** Appropriately, the preference of Jesus’ innocent human soul is to avoid the torment of being forsaken by His Father as He bears the guilt of others’ sin on the cross. Yet the eternal Son has assumed humanity in order to do God’s will, which centers on His offering His body (Heb. 10:5–10). Confronted now with the full cost of His obedient resolve, He completes His utter submission to God’s will in the covenant of redemption.
In spite of noble intentions (14:29, 31), Peter, like James and John, is incapable of one hour of true discipleship.

This exhortation recalls the warning of 13:32–37 to watch and not fall asleep before the coming of the Son of Man. Temptation is the trap of Satan to cause God’s people (in this case the Twelve) to fall and, if possible, to bring to nothing the plan of redemption.
Probably a force sent by the Sanhedrin, since the three categories of members of that body are mentioned (v. 53; 8:31 note).
A sign of respect that disciples showed to teachers in that day. After eating from the same dish (v. 20 note), Judas now feigns submission and respect.

The Greek can mean either “robber” or “insurrectionist,” but in view of the charges brought against Jesus at His trial (Luke 23:2), “insurrectionist” is better. The same term describes those crucified with Jesus (Mark 15:27), and they (as well as Barabbas, who was released instead of Jesus, 15:7) were probably also condemned as terrorist insurgents.
See note on 8:31. In view of v. 50, the passage Jesus has in mind may be Zech. 13:7 (see v. 27).

Some interpreters have suggested that in this cryptic detail, as in the mention of the linen garment (a sign of wealth), there might be a veiled reference to Mark himself, since he was from a well-to-do family in Jerusalem (Acts 12:12). At least he identified himself closely enough with Jesus’ group that the authorities tried to seize him. Yet he, like the Eleven, escaped, leaving Jesus in the custody of enemies.

This section of the narrative concerns Jesus’ trials before the Jews and the Romans, which were full of errors and irregularities, with the principles of justice subordinated to expediency and politics. The Jewish trial had three parts: a hearing before Annas (reported only in John 18:12–14, 19–23); a trial before the Sanhedrin, led by Caiaphas in his house (14:53–65); and an early morning session of the Sanhedrin (15:1). The Roman trial was likewise in three parts: before Pilate (15:2–5); before Herod Antipas (reported only in Luke 23:6–12); and before Pilate again (15:6–15).

Normally in Jesus’ day, the Sanhedrin would hold its sessions in the marketplace near the temple. This trial takes place in the high priest’s residence. The trial is irregular in time (at night) and place and in its unusual haste.

Deut. 19:15–21 requires that for guilt to be established, there must be two or three corroborating witnesses. False witnesses are to receive the same punishment as the accused. These regulations are not followed in the trial of Jesus.

verse_quote: I will destroy this temple that is made with hands.
note: The first three (Synoptic) gospels do not record Jesus saying anything resembling this. However, in John’s account of the temple cleansing, Jesus says that His enemies (not He) will destroy “this temple” (His body) and that He will raise it up in three days (John 2:19). This supports the probability that Christ cleansed the temple twice, since the lapse of three years would explain the false witnesses’ garbled version. See note on Matt. 26:59–61 for why these witnesses are “false” in their testimony against Jesus.

As the submissive and suffering Servant of the Lord, Jesus maintains silence, refusing to defend Himself and to repay insult with insult (Is. 53:7; 1 Pet. 2:23).

**Christ.** From the Gk. word meaning “anointed one.” “Messiah” is the Hb. word of the same meaning (1 Sam. 2:10 note).

**Son of the Blessed.** “The Blessed” is an indirect substitute for “God,” used by the Jews to avoid the risk of taking God’s name in vain. The whole title means “Son of God” and in the context indicates royal messiahship rather than absolute divinity.

Asked point-blank about His messianic identity, Jesus answers frankly. See notes on 6:50; 13:6.

**Son of Man.** See note on 2:10. Jesus modifies the title “Messiah” in terms of the divine figure of Dan. 7.

**clouds of heaven.** The fact that the high priest will see evidence of the Son of Man’s enthronement supports the view that Jesus’ prophecy of the Son of Man’s coming in 13:24–27 refers to the destruction of Jerusalem and the growth of the church among the Gentiles.

A symbolic gesture expressing shock, sorrow, or horror (Gen. 37:29; 2 Kin. 18:37; 19:1; Ezra 9:3; Jer. 36:24; Joel 2:13).

**What further witnesses.** The high priest makes the whole Sanhedrin witness to what he considers Jesus’ blasphemy.

Jesus is condemned not for insurrection but for His claim to deity, the essence of His message. The prescribed punishment for blasphemy (insulting the honor of God’s name) according to Jewish law is death by stoning (Lev. 24:16), but in Jesus’ day only Roman courts can order capital punishment. Thus, Jesus will die by crucifixion, a Roman punishment (John 18:31, 32 and notes).

verse_quote: spit on him and ... strike him.
note:
In their agreement with the accusation of the high priest, all the members of the Sanhedrin condemn Him (v. 64), and some express their hostility with physical violence and personal insult. Spitting in the face indicates exclusion from the group (Num. 12:14, 15), as if by ritual defilement. As the Lord’s Servant, Jesus does not hide His face from disgrace and spitting (Is. 50:6). At this point, the Sanhedrin breaks decisively with the Messiah.

**Prophesy.** Since Jesus has been acclaimed as a prophet (6:15; 8:28; Luke 7:16), His tormentors challenge Him to exercise that gift by naming those who strike Him, though His head is covered.
In the first century, Nazareth was dismissed as a backwater town from which no one of significance would come (John 1:46). See note on 1:24.

The Jews of Judea hold the Galilean Jews in contempt as culturally and religiously inferior (John 7:52). Peter’s manner and accent give him away, especially in the courtyard of a Sadducean aristocrat.

Cowed twice by a servant girl and now by a bystander, Peter invokes God’s wrath to strengthen his repudiation of Jesus: “I do not know this man.” Immediately a second rooster crow reminds Peter of Jesus’ sober prediction (v. 30), which has been fulfilled precisely. Shocked at his cowardice and overwhelmed with shame, he weeps.

verse_quote: as soon as it was morning.
note:
Probably at dawn. The purpose of the new meeting is apparently to draw up a political charge that will lead the Roman authorities to condemn and execute Jesus (see Luke 23:2).

**Pilate.** The Apostles’ Creed mentions Pilate as the representative of Rome who faces Jesus in this trial. Pilate was Roman governor of Judea from A.D. 26 to 36. As magistrate, only he had the legal right to pronounce capital sentences (14:64 note).

Pilate’s question implies that the Sanhedrin’s charge is that Jesus’ claim to kingship subverts Rome’s authority over its subjects in Judea, Galilee, and elsewhere. The title itself is ambiguous. In a political sense, the Herods are kings and Jesus is not. Nevertheless, Jesus is King of the Jews, offered to them as the fulfillment of their messianic hopes.

**You have said so.** Though indirect, Jesus’ reply will naturally be interpreted as affirming the identification implied in Pilate’s question.

Pilate apparently wants to make Jesus realize that, before the law, silence means consent to all the charges being lodged against him by the Sanhedrin’s representatives. Again the Servant of the Lord maintains silence in the face of His enemies (cf. 14:61; Is. 53:7).

Apparently he is an insurrectionist who has sought the military overthrow of Rome. Matt. 27:16 (in some manuscripts) gives his first name as “Jesus” (Hb. “Joshua”), a common name of the period. The choice Pilate proposes to the crowd (v. 9) is unwittingly ironic: Jesus Barabbas, the would-be political savior of Israel, or Jesus of Nazareth, the true Savior of the world.

Of Persian origin and adopted by the Romans, this cruel and shameful form of capital punishment was used mainly against rebellious slaves and insurrectionists. Metal spikes were driven through the wrists or hands (John 20:25) and heels of the victim, who suffered terrible pain. Death usually resulted over the course of days from the effects of the injuries, hunger, dehydration, muscle fatigue, and exposure. Breaking the condemned’s legs (John 19:33) caused rapid death by asphyxiation, since the legs could no longer lift the body to help the person breathe. As Paul notes, the crucifixion of Jesus identified the form of His execution with being “hanged on a tree,” identified in the law of Moses as a sign of death under the curse of God (Gal. 3:13; see Deut. 21:23).
In Roman custom crucifixion was preceded by the act of flogging with a leather whip that had sharp pieces of bone and metal at the end of its lashes.

Originally the word for a military headquarters or barracks generally. In the Gospels it refers to an official residence (see Acts 23:35).

**whole battalion.** Lit. “cohort,” the tenth part of a Roman legion, consisting of approximately six hundred men.

verse_quote: clothed him in a purple cloak.
note:
In Jesus’ day, purple is expensive and hard to produce, and for this reason is a mark of high rank (Esth. 1:6; Prov. 31:22; Luke 16:19; Rev. 17:4), especially of royalty (2 Chr. 2:7, 14; 3:14; Song 3:10). The cruel troops spare no expense to mock Jesus’ acknowledgment that He is King of the Jews.

**crown of thorns.** Jesus bears the divine curse (v. 13 note) on the ground, which has produced thorns since Adam’s fall (Gen. 3:17, 18). The soldiers use the crown to ridicule the idea that Jesus was a king.
This salutation and the homage paid (v. 19) are mockeries of the respect due to royalty.

Cyrene was an important city in what is today Libya. There was a large Jewish settlement in Cyrene going back several hundred years (Acts 6:9).

**Alexander and Rufus.** Since Matthew and Luke also name Simon but only Mark mentions his sons, they may have been members of the Christian community to which Mark wrote, probably at Rome (see Rom. 16:13).

**carry his cross.** Usually the condemned man carries the crossbeam, weighing thirty to forty pounds. Simon, in taking up Jesus’ cross, becomes a visual image of the true discipleship that Jesus demands (8:34).
An ominous name, possibly referring to the shape of the hill where executions are carried out but also reinforcing its association with death.

A primitive form of painkiller. Jesus’ refusal of this mild anesthetic mixture signals His resolve to endure the horrors of the cross fully conscious of the pain. Later in the afternoon, to fulfill Scripture, He will accept a sip of bitter wine (John 19:28, 29; Ps. 69:21). Myrrh was an expensive spice used as a cosmetic in the first century. It was offered to Jesus at His birth as a gift for a king (Matt. 2:11) and used in His burial by Nicodemus (John 19:39, 40).

These are the spoils reserved for the execution squad. This seemingly unimportant detail is a fulfillment of Ps. 22:18, which describes the agony of a violent and undeserved death, suffered by one forsaken by God (Ps. 22:1, 16).
About nine a.m.

Called the _titulus_ in Latin, this was a sign carried before the prisoner on the way to execution and affixed to the cross over his head.

**The King of the Jews.** The charge is true, though not in the sense that the executioners understand it.

Though the Gk. word often means “robber,” it can also mean “insurrectionist” (14:48 note) or more generally “criminal.” Since robbery was not punishable by crucifixion under Roman law (v. 13 note), one of the latter two meanings is more probable here.

**15:28** This verse is lacking in the most ancient manuscripts, although it is present in the majority of existing manuscripts. Since Jesus was obviously “numbered with the transgressors” as He hung on a cross between two brigands or terrorists, it is possible that early copyists inserted the citation of Is. 53:12, based on the parallel passage of Luke 22:37.

verse_quote: destroy the temple and rebuild it.
note: Observers pick up the garbled report that false witnesses presented during the Sanhedrin’s nighttime hearing, using it to taunt Jesus. See note on 14:58.

This is both an insult and a diabolical temptation similar to those proposed to Jesus at the beginning of His ministry (Matt. 4:2–6). The devil is still seeking to subvert the work of redemption at the very moment of its accomplishment, when Jesus is at His greatest physical weakness (14:38).

verse_quote: He saved others; he cannot save himself.
note: Oblivious to the irony of their words, the chief priests and scribes speak truly: because the Son of Man has come to seek and save the lost (Luke 19:10), He has no other course but to lay down His life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).

Noon.

**darkness.** This recalls the darkness in Egypt, which lasted three days before the death of the firstborn sons (Ex. 10:22). See also the prophecy of Amos 8:9, 10, where the Lord promises to “darken the earth in broad daylight” in a time “like the mourning for an only son”; and Joel 2:30, 31, part of a larger prophecy to be fulfilled in the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21).

**ninth hour.** About three p.m.

Aramaic of the first verse of Ps. 22. Even near death, Jesus’ life is determined by what is written in Scripture. Again Mark preserves the Semitic wording of the tradition and then translates it for his Gentile readers.

Some mistake the word _Eloi_ for “Elijah,” perhaps because in some circles during that day it is believed that Elijah would return (6:15; 8:28; 9:11–13). This belief is based on an overly literal reading of Mal. 4:5, 6, a prediction fulfilled in John the Baptist’s ministry (cf. Matt. 17:9–13).

A cheap wine that has almost become vinegar. Unlike the offer of wine and myrrh (v. 23), there is no humanitarian desire to relieve the suffering here but rather a cruel intention to prolong it by reviving Jesus in order to see if “Elijah” would come at His call.

From the parallel order in John’s account, it appears that the loud cry is, “It is finished” (John 19:30). Jesus has been hanging on the cross for six hours (vv. 25, 34). Crucifixion might last two or three days (v. 13 note), but He voluntarily lays down His life. He gives up His life at the moment He chooses; no one can take it from Him (John 10:17, 18).

verse_quote: the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.
note: The downward direction of the tear shows that it is God’s act. It is likely that Mark is referring to the veil separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, which may have been as much as eighty feet (24 m) tall. The death of Jesus is the final and definitive sacrifice for sin (Heb. 7:27). The old covenant administration of the covenant of grace is brought to a decisive end. No longer will the high priest need to enter into the Most Holy Place behind the veil to atone for the sins of the people (Ex. 26:31–33; cf. Heb. 9:1–10). Jesus is the new and eternal High Priest (Heb. 8:1), and also the perfect sacrificial victim (Heb. 9:14) who obtains for His people “eternal redemption” (Heb. 9:12). By means of His sacrificed body, believers of all tribes and races may now pass through the veil into God’s presence in prayer and worship (Heb. 10:19–22).

A Roman officer responsible for one hundred men. This centurion is apparently responsible for the detachment that puts Jesus to death. He is well placed to observe the death of Jesus.

**Son of God.** The Greek can be translated “a son of God.” A Roman would not typically see in this term the OT Messiah nor the eternal Son of the Trinity but rather the Hellenistic idea of a human being favored by the gods. Nevertheless, the confession stands as the goal and climax of Mark’s gospel, filled with the content of the Christian message, now confessed by a Gentile (see 1:1), who has been witness to Jesus’ suffering, crucifixion, and death.

That is, from Magdala on the southwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee. Jesus earlier cast seven demons out of Mary (Luke 8:2).

**Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses.** Known only from this incident (cf. 16:1; Matt. 27:56).

**Salome.** Mother of James and John (Matt. 27:56; cf. Matt. 20:20, 21).

All the men have fled except for the beloved disciple (John 19:26, 35). These women will come to the tomb two days later, intending to anoint Jesus’ corpse, only to be told that He has risen from the dead (cf. 16:1, 9; John 20:11–18).

The day before the Sabbath (Friday; John 19:14 note). Food is prepared before sunset, when the Sabbath begins. Joseph must buy the linen, make arrangements for Jesus’ burial, and ready the tomb (vv. 43–46) in the three hours remaining between Jesus’ death and sunset.

Perhaps from Ramah in Judea, twenty miles (32 km) northwest of Jerusalem, the city of the prophet Samuel (1 Sam. 1:1). See note on Luke 23:50, 51.

**council.** Joseph did not concur with the Sanhedrin’s (8:31 note) verdict to condemn Jesus (Luke 23:50, 51).

**looking for the kingdom of God.** Like Simeon and Anna and others, Joseph’s longing for the arrival of God’s reign met its fulfillment in Jesus (Luke 2:25, 38). See note on 1:15. Joseph is no doubt a pious Pharisee but also a secret follower of Jesus (John 19:38).

**took courage.** This is apparently Joseph’s first act of faith, but it comes at a time when all Jesus’ disciples have fled. Joseph puts himself in conflict with the decision of the Sanhedrin and jeopardizes his entire future.
Pilate’s surprise at how quickly Jesus dies provides more confirmation of the unusual character of Jesus’ death as a voluntary sacrifice (v. 37 note).

verse_quote: tomb ... cut out of the rock.
note: According to Matt. 27:60, the tomb belongs to Joseph and his family. Such a family burial site would consist of an ornately painted vestibule from which a passageway leads to individual benches or shelves cut into the rock where the bodies are laid. The tomb is sealed by a heavy stone that is rolled along a groove cut into the rock at the entrance.

At sunset (six p.m.) on Saturday evening, a time appropriate for buying spices but not for visiting tombs.

**anoint.** Anointing is a way of showing respectful affection in that day (14:8 note).

verse_quote: Who will roll away the stone.
note: They saw the “very large” (v. 4) stone put in its place (15:46 note) and now wonder how it will be moved in order for them to do their work.

They enter the vestibule of the burial chamber, at the far end of which is the individual niche (a bench or shelf) where Jesus’ body was laid (15:46 note).

**young man.** Matt. 28:2 says the women met an angel at the tomb.

If this gospel reaches its climax in the confession that Jesus is the Son of God (15:39 note), a second climax is reached with the declaration of His resurrection, which attests that His many predictions of His suffering and resurrection are true (8:31; 9:31; 10:34; 14:25, 28) and that God’s kingdom has come in power.

These two words make all the difference in the enormous role that Peter plays in the subsequent history of redemption. By them Mark indicates, as he brings his gospel to an end (16:9–20 note), that Jesus’ work of preparation of the Twelve has not been in vain. Other gospels also attest Jesus’ special care to restore the apostle who denied Him three times (Luke 24:34; John 21:15–23).

**he is going before you to Galilee.** See note on 14:28. Since this rendezvous is predicted twice, first by Jesus and now by the angel at His empty tomb, it is striking that neither the widely attested “longer ending” of Mark (vv. 9–20) nor the later “shorter ending” records an appearance of Jesus to His disciples in Galilee. (Other gospels locate the appearances mentioned in vv. 9–20 in Jerusalem and its environs.)

If vv. 9–20 are not original (see introduction and note on 16:9–20), the gospel of Mark ends with this sentence. This is a surprising conclusion for a document that purports to be a “gospel,” a proclamation of “good news.” An opposing consideration is that the word translated “afraid” also means “reverential fear,” and the same state of mind is produced in the disciples at the sight of Jesus’ transfiguration (9:6), a type of the future resurrection.

Scholars differ regarding whether these verses were originally part of this gospel. Some important early Gk. manuscripts and ancient versions lack these verses, but many more manuscripts and versions include vv. 9–20 (known as the “longer ending”). One Latin manuscript has a “shorter ending” (roughly one verse long), which records the women’s reporting to Peter and others and then sums up Jesus’ sending His apostles from east to west to preach the gospel. A few Gk. manuscripts from the seventh through ninth centuries A.D. include both the shorter ending and the longer ending. Because of these differences among manuscripts and stylistic variance between vv. 9–20 and the rest of the gospel, many scholars believe that vv. 9–20 were not written by Mark but added by a later copyist. On the other hand, these verses are cited by writers from the late second century and are found in the majority of existing Gk. manuscripts of Mark’s gospel. This abundance of external evidence (presence in so many early copies and translations) has persuaded some scholars that vv. 9–20 are authentic. Moreover, some find it hard to believe that Mark intended to end his gospel on the note of the women’s fear and silence, without recounting an appearance of the risen Lord Jesus. When all of the evidence is taken into consideration, however, it appears most likely that the gospel of Mark originally concluded at v. 8. If so, then the addition of vv. 9–20 was a copyist’s well-intentioned attempt to make sure Mark tells the complete story of what happened after Jesus’ resurrection. Such additions should not trouble us, for they are easily discerned through the practice of NT textual criticism because God has preserved for us the original text written by the apostles in a variety of manuscripts. See topical article “New Testament Textual Criticism” on p. 2369.

**16:9 Mary Magdalene.** See John 20:11–18 and note on Mark 15:40.

**cast out seven demons.** If vv. 9–20 are original, we would expect this detail, apparently drawn from Luke 8:2, to have appeared in an earlier mention of Mary (15:40 or 16:1).

Cf. Matt. 28:19.

**the whole creation.** Cf. Col. 1:23.
Cf. Acts 2:38, 39. See theological note “Infant Baptism” on p. 37.

All the things predicted here (except drinking deadly poison) are recorded in the NT, especially in Acts: cast out demons (Acts 5:16; 8:7; 16:18; 19:12); new tongues (2:1–11; 10:44–46; 19:6); serpents (28:3–5); lay hands on the sick(9:12; 28:8). Stories about some of the apostles surviving being forced to drink poison are found in early Christian literature outside the Bible., 18
A position symbolizing the authority that Jesus shares with God the Father (14:62; Phil. 2:9; see Ps. 110:1). Cf. Luke 24:50, 51; Acts 1:9–11; 2:33–35.
